He said those challenges raise legitimate questions about whether the country can responsibly accommodate a large number of additional people without placing further pressure on already strained public services.

The human rights lawyer said the issue deserves even greater consideration because many of the individuals being transferred to Liberia are coming from a socioeconomic environment significantly better than what they are likely to encounter upon arrival.

“The question, therefore, is not whether Liberia should close its doors,” Gongloe said. “It is whether we can responsibly provide decent living conditions, healthcare, housing, security and opportunities for those we receive without worsening the hardship already faced by ordinary Liberians.”

Gongloe ultimately urged the government to preserve Liberia’s reputation as a welcoming nation while ensuring that humanitarian commitments are supported by adequate resources and planning.

“Liberia should remain a welcoming country. But humanitarian generosity must be matched by humanitarian capacity,” he concluded.

World.title: Liberia: How a Gbarnga Tailor Built a School That Trains Hundreds and Offers a Model for Small Businesses in Rural Areas
World.content:
ACD Vocational Training Institute’s main building in Gbarnga, Bong County, houses its vocational training, school uniform production and literacy programs, with a business center operating on the ground floor. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/New Narratives

Summary:

ACD Vocational Training Institute in Gbarnga has trained hundreds of young people, especially women, over 25 years after starting with one borrowed sewing machine, creating pathways to employment and self-reliance without government or donor funding.

Despite its success, ACD faces challenges including high training costs, limited equipment and unpaid student fees, mirroring broader struggles in Liberia’s vocational training and small business sectors.

Experts say ACD’s self-sustaining model offers a blueprint for workforce development throughout the country, showing how local ownership and market partnerships can succeed without donor dependency.

By Nukanah Kollie with New Narratives

GBARNGA, Bong County —A bright blue two-story building stands in central Gbarnga, overlooking Broad Street. Red railings surround the balcony, where freshly sewn school uniforms hang beneath a sign reading, “ACD Vocational Training, School Uniform Production, Literacy Program.”

Inside, shelves hold colorful fabrics as sewing machines hum across the center. Founder Joseph M. Kamara, 66, sits on a wooden bench behind a black sewing machine, a measuring tape around his neck, turning cloth into uniforms while leading the self-financed vocational campus he has built over 25 years.

“I think the best thing to do for our people is impact knowledge in them,” said Kamara as he inspected a uniform completed by one of his employees. “When we talk about empowerment, I think the best empowerment is what gives them skills.”

Kamara has grown Accelerated Career Development Incorporated, known as ACD, which from a single borrowed sewing machine in 2001 into a two-campus institution that produces school uniforms sold across the region and creates opportunities for hundreds of women and young people.

Today, the school trains students in professional tailoring, driving, satellite installation, catering, hairdressing and weaving. It has grown at a time when experts say practical skills training is increasingly important in Liberia. The 2022 Liberia Population and Housing Census found that more than half of rural Liberians have no formal education, while rural literacy stands at 44 percent.

Nationally, Liberia’s vocational training sector has grown through international partnerships. A mid-term evaluation of the €25 million ($29 million) Youth Rising Project which ran from 2018 – 2024 rated the program as “satisfactory” but flagged heavy reliance on outside funding and gaps in graduate support.

Liberia’s private sector is dominated by small businesses. The World Bank’s 2024 Liberia National Establishment Census counted more than 40,000 businesses nationwide, 86 percent of them micro-enterprises. Development experts say their growth is a key factor in job creation and economic stimulation. But the World Bank has found that entrepreneurs continue to face limited access to finance, high interest rates and unreliable electricity.

Abraham Tumbey, a staff member at the UN Development Program, said vocational training is critical to addressing Liberia’s youth and female unemployment in a post-conflict economy where formal education cannot scale fast enough to absorb the labor force.

Joseph M.Kamara, founder of ACD Vocational Training Institute, works at a sewing machine in the school’s uniform store in Gbarnga, Bong County. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/New Narratives.

A School Built Almost Entirely By Women, For Women

Roughly 90 percent of ACD’s students are women, many of them single mothers. Kamara said the imbalance is intentional. The last Demographic and Health Survey in 2020 found that women head about one in three Liberian households, carrying the burden of supporting their families alone. Of the 107 students who have completed ACD’s full three-year tailoring program since 2001, about 96 percent have been women.

“Many of the men, they born by women, they leave the children with them, they go by their business, and the women struggle,” Kamara said.

For many women, the training was less about learning a trade than reclaiming independence. Patience Kollie, 40, a mother of three, completed ACD’s tailoring course before becoming an instructor in 2019 after the father of her children left the family.

“I want to tell all women out there who may be facing hard times,” she said. “Whether ACD can help you or people can help you, if you are serious, you can even pay your school fees yourself.”Martha Paye, 26, a mother of two and eight months pregnant, became an instructor in 2022 after her partner abandoned the family.

Former graduate and instructor Martha Paye, eight months pregnant, works alongside her colleagues at ACD’s new space known as “Annex Two”. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/ New Narratives.

“I decided to come to ACD to learn something, at least to help myself, because there was no support,” she said. “If I say I won’t go to school, we shall not have anybody to send me to school, and it will be suffering for myself.”

Korpo Boakai, another graduate turned instructor, said the training transformed her life.

“I able to support my home,” she said. “I’m trying to do something good for my children, and I change my life. I able to support my three children.”

Beyond tailoring: uniforms, employment and a growing footprint

The institution has relied on commercial bank loans seven times over the years to sustain and expand operations rather than turning to donor funding. He said the key to his success has been being careful with money.

“When you are doing business, you don’t play with the business money. We have always been very careful with it, not to tamper with it. We also go around looking for contracts, and the people we are training are our manpower.”

Kamara said professional tailoring is the course ACD can guarantee leads to work because graduates are absorbed into the school’s own production operations, including a uniform business that has grown into a storefront on Broad Street.

Tumbey said connecting graduates directly to production contracts turns capability into capital.

“Training alone does not put food on the table, market access does,” he said.

The scale is significant. Kamara said ACD partnered with the American Institutes for Research on a contract to produce 17,500 sets of school uniforms distributed across Bong, Lofa, Margibi and Grand Bassa counties. The school has also trained students in Bong, Margibi, Montserrado and parts of Lofa County.

It manufactures graduation gowns annually for Cuttington University. Workers, paid every two weeks based on output, earned a combined US$4,320 producing gowns and hats for Cuttington in June 2025 alone.

Aaron G.V. Juahkollie, Executive Director of the Foundation for International Dignity, said ACD has achieved what many vocational institutions struggle to do: survive without unreliable and unpredictable donor funding.

“The sustainability of any organization is what matters,” he said. “With the fact that they are sustaining themselves up to now, I think they are to be emulated, and government needs to look at them too, especially for the skills they are providing to women in the community.”

He pointed to ACD’s uniforms, tax compliance and 25 years of operation as proof of its credibility.

Persistent struggles faced by all small businesses

Without support from government or donors building the business has been challenging.

“Every day we beg, we go online, we look for people to help this program,” Kamara said.

He listed recurring challenges: high material costs, difficulty paying instructors and students struggling to complete tuition. Students unable to pay can work off fees once advanced enough to contribute to production.

Students echoed those concerns, describing a lack of personal sewing machines and difficulty accessing water.

“We don’t have, money and water around here,” Paye said. Like everyone here. She is hoping some benefactor will step up. “If they can help us with a water pump… that can help us to carry our school far, we’ll be happy.”

Tumbey has recommended that government make available low-interest micro-loans for small businesses like ACD, along with government investment in rural infrastructure – roads, electricity, water access – and tax incentives for businesses that hire and train young people.

One of the newly constructed buildings at ACD vocational training institute’s Annex Two in Gbarnga, Bong County. Credit: Nukanah Kollie

A school uniform for the future

Kamara said ACD’s ambition is to expand uniform production into a full factory capable of supplying government schools nationwide.

“Our first target is government schools,” he said. “We want to target government schools so that any government school in the republic… everything about school uniform, we’re going to produce.”

Tumbey called ACD an example other Liberian entrepreneurs could replicate, proving a movement does not require a massive grant; it can begin with a single borrowed machine.

ACD’s growth continues largely through word of mouth and Kamara’s outreach on local radio, where he encourages young people, particularly women, to enroll.

“If you don’t have any skill in your head, you have no hope,” he said. “But if you get skill in your head as you’re moving, you have hope that you will get something to do.”

Twenty-five years after beginning with one borrowed sewing machine, Kamara’s experiment has become far more than a tailoring school. It is a business, a training center and a source of opportunity for women and young people who might otherwise struggle to find a livelihood.

“You live by what you learn,” Kamara said.

This story is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” Reporting Project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The donor had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Weah Consoles Guinea After Conakry Landfill Landslide Kills 30
World.content:
Paynesville — Former Liberian President George Manneh Weah has extended condolences to Guinea’s President Mamady Doumbouya and the people of Guinea following a devastating landslide at a major landfill in the capital, Conakry, that killed at least 30 people and critically injured six others.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The disaster occurred early Sunday, August 24, when heavy rains triggered a landslide at the Dar es Salaam landfill, a massive open-air waste dump in Conakry. The collapse buried nearby makeshift structures and destroyed several homes.

In a statement issued Tuesday, August 25, the Office of Former President Weah said he conveyed his “profound condolences” to President Doumbouya, the Guinean government and, particularly, families affected by the tragedy.

Weah also wished those injured a speedy recovery, saying he shared in the grief of the Guinean people during what he described as a difficult national moment.

“It is my fervent prayer and hope that you, your Government and the people of the Republic of Guinea, including, but not limited to the bereaved and affected families, in your usual resilience, will take solace in God The Almighty, as you go through this challenging national period of your existence,” Weah said in his message.

Disaster Strikes Before Landfill Closure

The landslide reportedly occurred shortly after 2 a.m. GMT on Sunday following heavy rainfall. Authorities said the rains washed over the enormous heap of refuse at Dar es Salaam, causing the unstable waste pile to collapse onto nearby dwellings.

Authorities launched a search-and-rescue operation to locate possible survivors. Six people were reported seriously injured, while several homes were destroyed.

The landfill had reportedly been designated for closure on Sunday, according to Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, a sanitation official with Guinea’s military engineering battalion.

The disaster has drawn renewed attention to the dangers posed by informal settlements around large waste dumps, particularly during Guinea’s rainy season.

Weah Praises Guinean Resilience

In his condolence message, Weah expressed confidence that President Doumbouya, his government and the Guinean people would overcome the tragedy with renewed strength and hope.

He said Guinea’s resilience would help the country navigate the aftermath of the disaster and urged the affected families to find comfort in their faith.

The former Liberian leader’s message comes as rescue workers and authorities continue efforts to respond to the deadly landslide and assess the full extent of the destruction in Conakry.

Weah concluded by assuring President Doumbouya and the Guinean people of his solidarity as they mourn those who lost their lives.

World.title: PUL Revives Blyden Forum as Top Experts Tackle Liberia’s Drug Trafficking Crisis
World.content:
Monrovia – The Press Union of Liberia is set to relaunch its flagship intellectual platform, the Edward Wilmot Blyden Intellectual Discourse, with a high-level panel discussion focused on Liberia’s escalating drug trafficking crisis and the urgent need to strengthen institutions, accountability and the rule of law.

The forum, scheduled for Wednesday, August 26, comes as Liberia confronts the fallout from major cocaine seizures and growing public concern over the country’s capacity to investigate and prosecute complex drug trafficking cases.

The inaugural edition of the relaunched Blyden Forum will be held under the theme: “Confronting Drug Trafficking: Strengthening Institutions, Advancing Accountability, and Safeguarding the Rule of Law.”

Five prominent voices from government, the legal profession, civil society and the media will lead the discussion.

The panel includes Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh; Gbarpolu County Senator and Chairman of the Senate Committee on Audits and Public Accounts, Amara M. Konneh; President of the Liberia National Bar Association, Cllr. F. Juah Lawson; Executive Director of the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL), Anderson Miamen; and Infinity Broadcasting Corporation (Power FM & TV) Chief Executive Officer Aaron Kollie.

The discussion is expected to examine Liberia’s institutional response to drug trafficking, the effectiveness of ongoing investigations and prosecutions, accountability within law enforcement and justice institutions, and safeguards necessary to protect due process and the rule of law.

The forum also comes amid intense national debate over Liberia’s handling of the multimillion-dollar cocaine investigations, including questions about accountability, transparency and the independence of institutions responsible for enforcing the law.

According to the PUL in a release issued by its President Julius Kanubah, the forum is intended to provide a platform for informed and factual discussion of issues of national importance while bringing together policymakers, civil society actors, academics, journalists and media practitioners.

Named after Edward Wilmot Blyden, the pioneering Liberian journalist, intellectual and statesman, the forum is designed to generate expert perspectives, deepen public understanding and contribute to national policymaking through constructive dialogue.

The PUL said the platform will focus broadly on democratic governance, transparency, accountability and the rule of law—principles it considers essential to Liberia’s long-term stability and development.

The program begins at 11:00 a.m. at the PUL headquarters on Warner Avenue, 9th Street, Sinkor, Monrovia. Guests have been requested to be seated by 10:45 a.m.

World.title: Liberia: AFL Wants 20% Women in Uniform, Takes Recruitment Drive to Sinoe
World.content:
GREENVILLE, Sinoe County — The Armed Forces of Liberia wants women in one of every five uniformed posts, a target that would require nearly tripling their share of the force, and it took that recruitment drive to Sinoe County.

Women make up about 7.5 percent of the AFL, and the government’s goal is 20 percent, according to Junior Aloysius Morris, senior policy analyst at the Ministry of National Defense, who is traveling with the outreach team.

The five-member team includes two enlisted women, Sgt. [Patricia Lincoln] and Sgt. Newton L. Newton, who are talking to women in the county about enlistment requirements, career paths and the work soldiers do. Also on the team are Morris; Boyee S. Mussah, the AFL public relations officer; and Menicond B. Yarkpazna, junior policy analyst at the Ministry of National Defense.

The team is pointing women toward professional training, promotion into leadership and selection for United Nations peacekeeping deployments, which carry allowances and overseas service that few other public-sector jobs in Liberia offer.

The gap the campaign is trying to close is wide and has narrowed slowly. Women hold 11.5 percent of officer positions and 7.1 percent of enlisted positions, according to the project documentation. The Gender and Security Sector National Taskforce put women at 3 percent of the AFL in 2017, then the lowest share of any Liberian security institution, meaning the force has added roughly four and a half percentage points in about nine years.

The Sinoe outreach falls under a project the Ministry of National Defense and the AFL launched with UN Women on Feb. 9, 2026, titled “Strengthening Armed Forces of Liberia’s women active participation in peace and security through deployment to peacekeeping missions,” financed by the Elsie Initiative Fund. Beyond recruitment, the project funds pre-deployment preparation for female and male soldiers, including basic computer training, and public campaigns intended to counter the view of soldiering as men’s work.

The effort rests on an assessment the AFL ran in September 2022 using the Geneva Centre for Security Sector Governance’s Measuring Opportunities for Women in Peace Operations methodology, which examined what inside the institution keeps women from being deployed. The project is also framed against U.N. Security Council Resolution 1325, which calls for more women in the institutions that prevent and settle conflict and in U.N. field operations.

The campaign is designed to reach all 15 counties, grouped into four regions, in phases determined by recruitment potential, population, the presence of secondary schools and universities, and how easily the team can move. Alongside community meetings, the campaign is to run through schools, universities, county authorities, religious leaders and women’s organizations.

Neither the ministry nor the AFL has said what the enlistment numbers from the campaign have been so far, or by what year it expects to reach 20 percent.

World.title: Reform Front Liberia Moves Civic Reform From Ideas to Action
World.content:
Founder and Executive Director: Doug Zack Miller

Paynesville – The Reform Front Liberia, Inc. (TRFLI) is taking its civic reform message beyond discussion and into practical action through a growing platform focused on civic education, public engagement, reading, community development and positive journalism.

Built on the belief that sustainable national progress begins with informed, responsible and engaged citizens, TRFLI is a nonprofit, nonpartisan civic organization committed to education, empowerment, accountability, civic responsibility and constructive national dialogue.

Educate. Empower. Engage. Reform.

During August and September 2026, TRFLI’s mission is taking shape through three flagship programs: TRFL Radio Prime, the Reading & Comprehension Initiative, and The Reformpreneur Magazine.

Together, the initiatives provide platforms through which Liberians can listen, learn, read, think, discuss and participate in efforts to build stronger communities and a stronger Liberia.

From Vision to Action

TRFLI believes reform cannot exist merely as a slogan. It must ultimately be reflected in the way citizens think, communicate, work, lead, learn and participate in their communities.

The organization is therefore developing practical civic platforms that reach Liberians through radio, community education and publishing.

TRFL Radio Prime Launched August 1

TRFL Radio Prime, the organization’s first major public program, officially launched on August 1, 2026.

The weekly program airs every Saturday from 4:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. on Blaze Radio 90.7 FM, providing a platform for civic education, public discussion and conversations about the responsibilities citizens share in Liberia’s development.

Radio Prime promotes informed citizenship, personal responsibility, accountability and constructive dialogue. Rather than viewing national development solely through the actions of government, TRFLI also asks: What responsibility does the citizen have in building the Liberia we want?

The program is sponsored by Uncle Z Spice International, Inc. (UZSII).

Reading & Comprehension Initiative Takes Education Into the Community

Three weeks after launching Radio Prime, TRFLI took another part of its mission directly into the community.

On August 22, 2026, the organization officially launched its Reading & Comprehension Initiative at Kids and Us Preparatory Elementary School in Jackson Hill, Rehab Community, Paynesville.

The initiative is designed to help young adults and adults strengthen practical reading and comprehension skills while building confidence in communication and critical thinking.

Participants engage with reading materials and exercises intended not simply to determine whether they can pronounce words, but whether they can understand, explain, question and apply what they have read.

TRFLI considers reading and comprehension essential to civic reform, arguing that access to information alone is not enough. Citizens must also be able to understand information, evaluate it critically and make informed decisions.

TRFLI in action: Participants engage in reading and comprehension exercises during the official launch of the initiative on August 22, 2026, at Kids and Us Preparatory Elementary School in Jackson Hill, Rehab Community, Paynesville.

“A citizen who can read, understand and think is a citizen who can build, lead and transform.”

The Reformpreneur Magazine Set for September Launch

TRFLI’s third flagship platform, The Reformpreneur Magazine, is scheduled to launch in September 2026.

The digital publication will expand the organization’s educational mission through articles, research, interviews, commentary and positive stories centered on Liberia and its people.

The magazine will cover issues including reform, entrepreneurship, education, agriculture and food security, leadership, civic responsibility, business, community development and the stories of Liberians working to create positive change.

TRFLI also expects the publication to contribute to a stronger culture of reading while connecting Liberians at home with the diaspora and friends of Liberia.

Three Programs, One Civic Mission

The three initiatives are designed to complement one another.

TRFL Radio Prime gives citizens a platform to listen, learn and engage.

The Reading & Comprehension Initiative provides an opportunity to read, understand, question and develop critical-thinking skills.

The Reformpreneur Magazine will provide a platform to read, learn, document ideas and share positive Liberian stories.

The organization describes the rollout as:

August 1: A voice for civic education.

A voice for civic education. August 22: Education in the community.

Education in the community. September: A platform for ideas, research and positive stories.

Why the Reform Front Liberia Was Established

TRFLI says Liberia’s future will depend not only on its political leadership but also on the quality of its citizens, institutions, businesses, educators, professionals, communities and civic organizations.

The organization was established around the conviction that national development requires responsibility at every level of society.

“Government has responsibilities. Institutions have responsibilities. Businesses have responsibilities. Community leaders have responsibilities. And citizens have responsibilities,” the organization says.

TRFLI seeks to encourage a culture in which Liberians become better informed, accept greater personal and civic responsibility, demand accountability appropriately, value education and reading, participate constructively in their communities and contribute solutions rather than merely identifying problems.

Nonpartisan, Civic and Educational

The Reform Front Liberia, Inc. emphasizes that it is not a political party or political campaign organization.

Its mission is civic and focuses on citizens, education, responsibility, accountability, entrepreneurship, community development and Liberia’s long-term progress.

The organization believes Liberians with different political views, backgrounds and experiences can find common ground around education, responsible citizenship, stronger institutions and national development.

Message From the Founder and Executive Director: Doug Zack Miller

Miller says Liberia’s transformation will require more than the efforts of any single individual, organization or government.

“Liberia’s transformation will not come from one person, one organization or one government. It will require citizens who are informed, responsible, educated and willing to participate in building their communities and their country.”

According to Miller, TRFLI was established because reform must move beyond conversation.

“We must educate, organize, build programs and demonstrate through action what responsible citizenship can accomplish.”

He said the organization’s three flagship programs are intended to provide different avenues for civic engagement.

“Radio Prime gives us a voice. Our Reading & Comprehension Initiative takes education directly into the community. The Reformpreneur Magazine will give us another platform to document ideas, entrepreneurship and positive Liberian stories.”

“We are starting deliberately and building step by step,” Miller added. “Our objective is not simply to talk about a better Liberia. We want to participate constructively in building one.”

What Comes Next

TRFLI says it intends to continue developing its programs carefully and sustainably, with an immediate focus on strengthening the three flagship initiatives already underway or scheduled for launch.

Radio Prime will continue its weekly civic education broadcasts, while the Reading & Comprehension Initiative will continue its community-based educational activities.

The first edition of The Reformpreneur Magazine is scheduled for September 2026.

As its organizational capacity grows, TRFLI says it will explore additional educational and community-impact programs consistent with its civic mission, with emphasis on sustainable initiatives with clear and achievable objectives.

An Invitation to Liberia and the Diaspora

The Reform Front Liberia is inviting citizens, educators, professionals, businesses, community organizations, young people, volunteers, Liberians in the diaspora and friends of Liberia to participate in its civic efforts.

Opportunities include volunteering, contributing professional expertise, partnering with programs, sponsoring initiatives and supporting the organization’s educational and community-impact activities.

TRFLI particularly welcomes businesses and institutions that view investment in education, informed citizenship and community development as an investment in Liberia’s future.

World.title: FRA set to open three Satellite depots in Mungwi
World.content:
The Food Reserve Agency (FRA) is set to open three additional satellite depots in Mungwi District in Northern Province this week.

This is in response to the surge in maize deliveries by farmers in the 2026 maize marketing season in the district.

Food Reserve Agency Northern Province Regional Marketing Coordinator, Timothy Chanda who disclosed the matter to ZANIS today said the additional depots will help increase the number of buying points from 38 to 41 in the district.

Mr Chanda noted that doing so is likely to hasten the buying process as well as help the agency cope with the growing volume of maize being delivered by farmers.

He said the expansion was necessary to ensure farmers deliver their produce efficiently without unnecessary delays.

“Mungwi District currently has 38 satellite depots, but looking at the number of farmers delivering their maize produce, we have been prompted to open three more depots this week we hope that by opening three more depots farmers can quicken their supply of maize to the Agency,” Mr Chanda said.

Mr Chanda disclosed that the additional satellite depots will be established in Tukuta and Misamfu areas, considering the large number of farmers in the area.

He has described the ongoing maize marketing season as progressive, adding that processing of payments for farmers is being done on a daily basis.

He has since urged farmers to adhere to schedules provided for by the Agency to ensure smooth and orderly operations at the depots.

Mr Chanda revealed that Mungwi district is among the major maize producing districts in Northern Province hence the need to increase buying points.

” Mungwi is one of the high maize producing district in the province, and the opening of the three additional satellites is targeted at high productivity areas in order to ease congestion and bring maize collection points closer to farmers, particularly those in far flung and high production areas,” he said.

The Food Reserve Agency is currently running the maize market, with huge stacks of maize being observed in many satellite depots across the district.

World.title: All is set for Kulonga traditional ceremony in Lundazi
World.content:
All is set for the Kulonga Traditional Ceremony of the Tumbuka people in Lundazi district, Eastern province.

The ceremony which is slated for September 12, 2026 will be celebrated under the theme: Our Culture brings about Peace and Unity to people.

Interpreting the theme, Kulonga Traditional Ceremony Organising Chairperson, Boyd Zimba says there can never be development without peace.

Mr Zimba says this is why the ceremony will serve as a platform to remind citizens of the importance of preserving peace and unity.

“As Tumbukas, we believe without unity and peace, there can never be development so people need to cherish the peace and unity that this country has enjoyed from time immemorial,” Mr Zimba stated.

Mr Zimba stated that Kulonga traditional which attracts Tumbuka speaking people of Muyombe and Malawi is originally celebrated during the last week of July, but was moved to second week of September due to the recently held general elections.

He added that the Malawi based Paramount Chief of the Tumbuka speaking people, Chikulamayembe will be in attendance, while an invitation has been extended to the office of the President to grace the occasion.

World.title: Kalulushi Pastors’ Fellowship congratulate HH on re election
World.content:
The Pastors Fellowship in Kalulushi has congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election for a second term, attributing the victory to the development delivered to the country.

Pastors Fellowship Kalulushi Chairperson, Reverend Clinton Longwani, told ZANIS in an interview in Kalulushi district that Zambians had no doubt in President Hichilema’s development agenda because there were visible projects to point to.

Rev Longwani said through the development projects the President had embarked on, the people of Zambia had expressed confidence in him and felt he deserved another mandate to complete what he started.

“We want to support the continuity of the free education policy, the school feeding program, and school bursaries for both public and private institutions. It is commendable work,” Rev Longwani said.

He added that as pastors in Kalulushi district, their prayer was that God grants President Hichilema wisdom to lead the nation.

He noted that the President had demonstrated leadership qualities that the country needs.

Meanwhile, Rev Longwani said the pastors in Kalulushi district have called on President Hichilema to help unite the country, noting that post-election issues can sometimes be traumatic.

World.title: Government commended swift payment of farmers
World.content:
The Kabwe Farmer’s Cooperative Society has commended Government for prompt payment of farmers who supply maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) during the ongoing crop marketing season.

Kabwe Farmer’s Cooperative Society Chairperson, Eugene Mwitumwa says the prompt payment of farmers will make it easy for the farming community to prepare for the 2026-2027 farming season.

Mr Mwitumwa said in an interview with the media that the move will motivate the farmers to boost their agricultural production in the forthcoming farming season.

“We are happy with the way payments are being done for the farmers who are selling their maize to the FRA and we wish to commend the government for ensuring that there are no delays,” Mr Mwitumwa said.

Mr Mwitumwa said the paying of farmers through commercial banks and mobile money platforms has helped in reducing congestion at banks.

“The queues we used to have at the farmers whenever farmers were being paid are no longer there because of the introduction of mobile money platforms,” he said.

He said the Kabwe Farmers Cooperative Society will continue supplementing the government’s efforts in enhancing national food security through the promotion of crop diversification.

Mr Mwitumwa said the agriculture sector has a bright future in Zambia because of the good agricultural policies being implemented in the country.

World.title: Govt. receives 100 fuel tankers
World.content:
Kinglong Motors Zambia Limited has handed over 100 fuel tankers to the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts, a move that will empower 12, 000 youths across the country.

Ministry of Youth, Sports and Arts Permanent Secretary Kangwa Chileshe described the fuel tankers as an important step towards transferring the assets to the beneficiary youth cooperatives.

He made the remarks during the handover ceremony of the fuel tankers at the National Sports Development Centre (NASDEC).

Mr Kangwa explained that the fuel tanker empowerment programme was launched in 2020 to address youth unemployment, increase the participation of local players in the petroleum sector and reduce the externalisation of profits by non-Zambian oil marketing companies.

Mr Chileshe said the programme was designed to empower young Zambians to participate in the importation and transportation of petroleum products, while promoting local wealth creation.

He said the programme was also expected to contribute to the reduction of petroleum prices and ensure that more profits from the sector are retained within the country.

Mr Chileshe says the 100 fuel tankers were procured from Kinglong Zambia Limited on a hire-purchase arrangement, with the government paying 50 percent of the total cost upfront and the balance structured for repayment over three years.

He explained that the programme was implemented in two phases, with the first 50 tankers arriving in 2021 and being allocated to 50 youth cooperatives operating under Kapesika and Mount Meru.

Mr Chileshe said another 50 tankers arrived in 2022 and were allocated to an additional 50 youth cooperatives, bringing the total number of beneficiary cooperatives to 100.

He has urged the beneficiaries to use the tankers as productive assets to build sustainable businesses, create employment and contribute to national economic growth.

Mr Chileshe reaffirmed the government’s commitment to ensuring that youth empowerment programmes translate into real economic opportunities, sustainable enterprises and improved livelihoods.

And Kinglong Motors Limited, General Manager Wu Chunming reaffirmed the company’s commitment to partnering with the government in promoting youth empowerment and economic development.

Mr Chunming said the occasion represents more than the handover of equipment, but a partnership aimed at creating meaningful economic opportunities for young people.

World.title: Chienge’s election victory reflects the electorates’ confidence
World.content:
United Party for National Development (UPND) Deputy Spokesperson, Elvis Nkandu says the party’s victory in the Chienge parliamentary seat and local government wards reflects the electorate’s confidence in the Government’s development agenda.

Mr Nkandu says the UPND’s victory demonstrates that residents are responding positively to the government’s efforts to improve infrastructure and social services.

UPND’s Favourite Musangu won the parliamentary seat in Chienge Constituency, while the party won five local government seats in Chienge and two in Kalungwishi Constituency.

“We are grateful to the people of Chienge, and this victory is a clear endorsement of the development agenda being implemented by the UPND Government,” Mr Nkandu said.

Mr Nkandu said the construction of the Nchelenge-Mununga-Luchinda road is among the major developmental projects demonstrating the Government’s commitment to improving connectivity in the area.

“For many years, people saw groundbreaking ceremonies, but very little happened on the ground. Today, people can see equipment and actual construction works taking place,” Mr Nkandu said.

Mr Nkandu said the party’s growing support in Luapula Province is also attributable to the expansion of social protection programmes, including increased coverage under the Social Cash Transfer and higher allocations under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

“Government has continued to put more resources into programmes that directly benefit communities, and the people are seeing these interventions,” he said.

He said the election outcome had also been accompanied by an increase in UPND membership and improved electoral margins in the constituency.

Mr Nkandu assured the people of Chienge that the UPND would not take the confidence placed in the party for granted.

“This trust is not a licence for us to relax. It is a responsibility to work even harder and ensure that development reaches more people,” he said.

World.title: Chief Chimese seeks early inputs
World.content:
Chief Chimese of the Ushi people in Mansa District has urged the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) and the Ministry of Agriculture to commence the distribution of farming inputs under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) before the onset of the rains.

In an interview with the media, Chief Chimese noted that by September and October, farmers will begin land preparation ahead of the rainy season.

He emphasised that in order for farmers to maintain the positive trajectory of maize production seen in the 2025/2026 farming season, farming inputs must be distributed on time to ensure timely planting.

“I am grateful to the government for the way the Food Reserve Agency is working. Our farmers are being paid on time, and this time around we are appreciating the electronic system of paying farmers via mobile money services. This is why even when it comes to inputs, they should be given on time,” said Chief Chimese.

The traditional leader further observed that the government needs to start empowering farmers with irrigation systems so that the country can produce maize all year round.

“We are doing well in production, and just as President Hakainde Hichilema has been talking about increasing maize output, we now need to seriously consider irrigation so that crop production continues throughout the year,” he said.

Meanwhile, a farmer at Mano Satellite Depot in Mansa District, Aaron Chanda, commended the Food Reserve Agency for paying farmers through mobile money services.

“Previously, we used to line up at banks for days before receiving our money. Now, farmers are paid via mobile money within three days,” he said.

Mr Chanda added that the initiative is commendable and urged that payment services be further improved to make the cost of doing business easier for farmers.

World.title: PIDACC boosts Mwinilunga mechanisation
World.content:
Government through the Program for Integrated Development and Adaptation to Climate Change (PIDACC) with support from the African Development Bank (AfDB) has over the last one year handed over an assortment of agriculture mechanisation equipment to three wards in Mwinilunga District of North-western Province.

The equipment which include three tractors, three rippers with calter and crumbler, three maize shellers, three Boom sprayers, three multicrop planters and three trailers have been procured at the cost of overK5.1 million.

District Agricultural Coordinator Lewis Chiwele said the agricultural equipment has been distributed to Chibwika, Ntambu and Kakoma wards to support farmers and build resilience against the effects of climate change.

Mr Chiwele explained that the equipment has brought about agricultural efficiency as farmers are now able to prepare their fields, harvest and shell their crop within a short period of time while implements such as trailers are being used to transport their farm produce to markets and satellite depots.

“This program has proven that this support can improve the efficiency of our farming operations, most of our farmers have had challenges to prepare their land, to harvest, to shell, now with this support our farmers are able to save time” he said.

He said the program is equally critical in contributing to the government’s target of 10 million metric tonnes of annual maize production by 2031 adding that farmers in the three wards are eager to utilize the equipment to increase their agriculture productivity.

Boaz Mukanzu a farmer in Kamfumbu area of Chibwika ward thanked the government for implementing the PIDACC project stating that it has afforded him efficiency and reduced production cost.

Mr Mukanzu said using the machinery, he was able to cultivate over three hectares within a day and shell his maize on time which previously took him months to do.

“We thank the government because this project has significantly reduced our manual labour and we now can shell maize or cultivate as much as three hectares in a day,” he said.

The PIDACC project targets to build resilience in farmers that are vulnerable to effects of climate change through mechanisation in communities along the Zambezi river basin.

World.title: Zambia: 'I Became Protective' - A Cancer Survivor's Fight to Fix Zambia's Health System
World.content:
"Once you go through something as traumatic as a cancer diagnosis, you automatically become protective of the next person," said Karen Nakawala, a Zambian broadcaster and cervical cancer survivor.

Nakawala knows that trauma firsthand. In 2019, her life changed when she was diagnosed with cervical cancer.

The diagnosis forced Nakawala to confront the disease she would later dedicate much of her life to talking about publicly. After treatment, she converted her experience into advocacy, determined to help other women recognize the importance of early screening and seeking care.

During her own treatment, she said she saw gaps throughout the healthcare system, with many women falling through the cracks, a realization that pushed her from patient to advocate. "I believe that cancer healthcare solutions should be culturally grounded given our diverse culture and should be rooted in those who live it," she said.

Through her journey, she created Teal Sisters Foundation, an organization that has become a platform for women to access information, share their experiences, and seek support without judgment. Her private Facebook community, initially created as a safe space where women could speak openly about their health without being judged, has grown to more than 137,000 members. The women-only Facebook community aims to boost access to cervical cancer screening, prevention and treatment in Zambia.

Cancer is an increasing burden in Zambia.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer indicates that cervical cancer is still the most prevalent form of cancer in the country, with 4,730 estimated new cases in 2024. It was also the most prevalent form of cancer causing death and accounted for 2,769 cancer-related deaths in the same year. Breast cancer was the second most prevalent form of cancer among women, with 1,555 estimated new cases and 730 deaths.

Zambia has the third-highest burden of cervical cancer in the WHO African Region after Eswatini and Malawi

There is also a huge shortage of specialists in the country. Ministry of Health data shows that Zambia has just six oncologists serving a population of about 20 million people. To help close this gap, Zambia has, since 2006, invested in training nurses to play a greater role in cervical cancer prevention and care, including screening, treatment and vaccination.

Against this backdrop, the reopening of the radiotherapy and imaging unit at Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital takes on particular significance.

For years, patients needing radiotherapy faced a major gap in the country's cancer-care system. Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital was shut down in 2020 for a major upgrade. Its closure left patients with fewer treatment options and forced them, in some cases, to seek care outside the country. Nearly 1,000 patients were left waiting for radiotherapy during the interruption, with about 600 referred to India for treatment, according to health authorities.

Nakawala described the six-year gap as "the worst period in Zambia's cancer healthcare space."

She said the country lost many women to breast and, in particular, cervical cancer, some diagnosed at early stages that could have been treated with good outcomes had radiotherapy been available. Those who could afford it traveled outside the country for treatment, she said, at "an astronomical out-of-pocket spend for families." That gap, she said, has left a large backlog of patients now waiting for treatment, placing pressure on the newly reopened unit.

Zambian Cancer Society/LinkedIn The opening of the refurbished radiotherapy and imaging section of the Cancer Diseases Hospital, Lusaka

Zambia's reopening of the radiotherapy and imaging cancer treatment facility at Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital pushed for better women's cancer care in Africa. The facility was upgraded and commissioned by President Hakainde Hichilema in August, 2026. It can now treat up to 60 patients a day.

For patients, the restoration of the service means that specialised cancer treatment can once again be accessed closer to home, reducing the delays, travel and financial pressure associated with seeking care abroad. The hospital's upgraded radiotherapy services include external beam radiotherapy, treatment planning and brachytherapy, supported by advanced imaging equipment.

"The first thing that comes to mind is the relief that patients and their caregivers feel," said Nakawala. "It is always better to receive treatment close to home where you are surrounded by loved ones."

Cancer treatment can be isolating, she said, and travelling abroad can deepen that isolation when patients cannot afford to take a caregiver with them. The reopening of the radiation unit therefore brings hope while potentially shortening treatment delays and reducing cancer mortality in the country.

Still, she cautioned that 60 patients a day "is not enough, but it is a positive step forward," and that treatment capacity should grow once the unit is fully operational. However, the government must ensure that there is a solid plan for servicing and reinvesting so that we get uninterrupted optimal operation and services, which will be much to the benefit of both government and patients, she added.

Hichilema said that the installation of advanced cancer treatment equipment at the Cancer Diseases Hospital in Lusaka is a major step towards positioning Zambia as a regional centre for cancer diagnosis and treatment. He said Zambia is now the third country in Africa, after South Africa and Egypt, to have the equipment, which will allow patients to access specialised cancer treatment locally rather than travelling abroad, including to India.

The reopening comes at a critical time for Zambia, where the burden of cancer continues to place pressure on an already stretched health system. The burdens of breast cancer, cervical cancer, and HIV are overlapping among women in low- and middle-income countries.

Nakawala said the six-year closure exposed how centralized cancer treatment has been in Zambia. Even when cancer was caught early, she said, most deaths during that period were driven by lack of access and delayed treatment, worsened whenever machines broke down, and treatment was interrupted - sometimes never resuming. She pointed to several consequences of the resulting gaps in services: late-stage diagnosis, as patients often wait to seek care until pain and side effects become advanced; higher mortality tied to delayed or absent treatment; and a heavier financial burden on the country, since sending patients abroad for treatment costs more than treating them at home.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women in sub-Saharan Africa, with an estimated 129 000 new cases in 2020.

Yet survival remains far lower than in high-income countries, with five-year survival estimated at around or below 50% in the region. The burden is expected to grow sharply, with the number of women diagnosed each year projected to nearly double by 2040. The African Breast Cancer – Disparities in Outcomes (ABC-DO) study found that 50% to 90% of women in different African countries are diagnosed when the cancer has already reached an advanced stage, when treatment is more difficult, and the chances of cure are lower.

According to the study, inadequate treatment access and late diagnosis are responsible for the poor outcomes. Many women recognise changes in their breasts and seek medical help, but face long waits before receiving a diagnosis and starting treatment.

WHO Africa Zambia steps up cervical cancer screening with HPV testing

In the study, half of women in Zambia and Namibia and three-quarters in Uganda reported having breast symptoms for more than six months. Survival at three years was just 46% among women in Zambia and Uganda, compared with 58% among Black women in Namibia and South Africa and 36% in Nigeria. The study estimates that more than one-third of breast cancer deaths in sub-Saharan Africa could be prevented through earlier diagnosis and timely access to high-quality treatment.

Nakawala attributed the same regional shortfall in equipment behind those numbers. "38% of countries in sub-Saharan Africa have no radiotherapy equipment at all," she said, "and 60-70% of women are diagnosed at a late stage."

She said five in ten women diagnosed with breast cancer in sub-Saharan Africa will not survive five years, compared with nine in ten who survive in high-income countries. She listed stigma, lack of awareness and information, financial constraints, distance, and limited access to screening and timely treatment as the biggest barriers keeping women from care.

"In Zambia, cervical cancer is the number one killer of women, yet it is highly preventable. It is followed by breast cancer, which, if caught early, can be treated with good outcomes," said Nakawala.

Breast cancer can also be treated with good outcomes when detected early.

Breast cancer, she said, is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women in Africa, with cases expected to double by 2040.

Zambia's ambition to become a regional centre of excellence in cancer care will therefore require more than a single upgraded facility. She said decentralization is essential so the burden doesn't fall entirely on the newly upgraded Lusaka unit. She added that two additional centres are under construction in Ndola to serve the northern region and in Livingstone to serve the south.

Beyond radiotherapy, Nakawala said government needs to work more closely with civil society organizations to raise awareness and share information with women, particularly given the gap created by years without radiation treatment. She called for greater investment in women's health and more equitable access to care. She said that Zambia should align more closely with the World Health Organization's Global Cancer Initiative to speed up early detection and diagnosis and improve survival.

She also pointed to the role of groups like the Africa Breast Cancer Council, of which she is a member, in helping governments strengthen advocacy, stakeholder engagement, and community efforts to reduce stigma by sharing best practices across member countries.

Nakawala argued that geography should not determine whether a woman survives cancer.

"No one single person should be disadvantaged because of their geographical location. We are all entitled to good healthcare services regardless of geography," she said.

She said that when the world talks about universal healthcare, it must reach beyond urban areas to everyone, which is why decentralizing cancer care matters so much. For Zambia and the wider region, that means bringing cancer services closer to the people who need them through greater investment, training and decentralisation.

"Let us all be intentional when it comes to cancer," Nakawala said. "Governments and international communities should support advocacy programmes which are centred on prevention and early diagnosis."

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 26, 2026
World.content:
Ramaphosa Vows Arrests Over Anti-Migrant Violence

President Cyril Ramaphosa has pledged that perpetrators of violence against foreign nationals will be arrested and prosecuted once police have gathered sufficient evidence. He rejected claims that the government tolerates xenophobia. Ramaphosa also denied that South Africa had been isolated by other African leaders over the recent violence. He said the country remained a respected pan-African actor. He said the government had engaged African leaders on migration and that regional cooperation was needed to address the underlying causes of migration, including insecurity and poor governance.

Nigeria Launches Manhunt After Mass Abductions

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who attacked four villages in Niger State. The attackers killed more than 40 people and abducted an unverified number of residents. Local officials said that as many as 500 people may have been taken. A video released by the kidnappers appeared to show some of the captives alive in a forest. Survivors have fled to neighbouring states and Benin. Others are receiving treatment for injuries. The attacks, which also involved improvised explosive devices, come amid growing insecurity in the region and concerns over the spread of jihadist groups along Nigeria's north-western border areas.

Anger Mounts After Deadly Guinea Landfill Collapse

Two days after a deadly landfill collapse in Guinea, rescuers are using giant excavators to search for victims. Anger is growing among residents who said that they had repeatedly warned authorities about the landfill's dangerous condition and urged its closure. At least 31 people have died, and more than 20 were injured after a landfill collapsed in Conakry's Dar es Salam neighbourhood following heavy rain. Hundreds of displaced residents are sheltering at a school, and dozens of households remain at risk. The site has been linked to previous deadly collapses and severe pollution. The government plans to replace it with a new landfill, which has been underway since 2022.

ICC Clears Libya Case for First Trial

The International Criminal Court has confirmed 17 charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity against former Libyan security official Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri. This paves the way for the first Libya-related case to reach trial since the ICC opened its investigation 15 years ago. El Hishri is accused of torture, rape, murder, enslavement and other abuses against Libyan and migrant detainees at Tripoli's Mitiga prison. Survivors and rights groups said that the case could expose the wider system of migrant detention and exploitation in Libya, including alleged links to European migration-control policies. They called for further investigations into the responsibility of European officials.

Close 

Interpol Arrests 58 in Global Cybercrime Operation

Interpol said 58 people linked to organised West African cybercrime networks have been arrested in a global operation targeting romance and investment scams across 22 countries and six continents. Operation Jackal IV, conducted between November 2025 and June 2026 and identified 263 suspects. It uncovered fraud involving cryptocurrency, email compromise, money laundering and sextortion, including the targeting of minors. In South Africa, police arrested 39 people, raided seven sites, and seized $2.67 million. They also blocked 257 bank accounts linked to a syndicate. Interpol said the operation highlights the growing global reach of networks such as Black Axe and the importance of international cooperation in disrupting their finances. Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network with trafficking, prostitution and killing operations around the world.

World.title: South Africa: Mogotsi Escape Plot Report Due in Court - South African News Briefs - August 26, 2026
World.content:
Mogotsi Escape Plot Report Due in Court

Self-proclaimed political fixer Brown Mogotsi’s alleged escape plot is set to return to court on 1 September, reports EWN. The case was postponed after the State could not produce a report from Correctional Services to prove his alleged attempt to break free. Mogotsi allegedly planned to disguise himself in a Correctional Services uniform and walk out of the Johannesburg Magistrates Court cells. He was removed from a police van before being taken to court and placed in leg irons, with security also tightened. Mogotsi has been in custody since May after failing to secure bail over allegations that he provided false addresses.

Gauteng Health Probes Bribery Allegations



The Gauteng Department of Health is investigating allegations that officials may be accepting bribes from patients in exchange for appointments, access to medical files and the collection of medication outside normal procedures, reports SABC News. Department spokesperson Steve Mabona condemned bribery, corruption and preferential treatment in public healthcare. He said that the allegations are serious enough to warrant an investigation into whether officials are soliciting or accepting payments from patients.

Biko Family Seeks Testimony From Apartheid Spy

The reopened inquest into the 1977 death of anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko could examine the role of former apartheid spy Craig Williamson, reports EWN. Biko’s family is seeking to have him subpoenaed. The family says Williamson’s previous evidence that Biko was under surveillance could help answer questions about what security forces knew before his death. Biko’s widow, Nontsikelelo, is also expected to testify about the surveillance operation. The family has requested more time to prepare her and review evidence from the original inquest and Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The court is expected to rule on the postponement request.

World.title: Africa: African Agriculture Offers Key Pathway to Economic Development and Jobs
World.content:
A Food and Agricultural Organization project supports capacity development to contribute to healthy cotton sectors and increase the incomes of cotton farming families in Burkina Faso, Mali, Senegal, Tanzania and Zambia.

Africa is home to about two thirds of the world's uncultivated arable land. It is blessed with an average of 300 days of sunshine annually. At a time when many of the world's advanced countries are experiencing population stagnation or decline, Africa with 1.6 billion people is the world's second largest continent. Its population is the fastest growing and the median age is 19.5 years.

About 60% of these people are employed in the agriculture sector and African countries are major producers of cocoa, coffee, tea, cassava, cotton and sweet potatoes.

Economic growth in 2026 is projected at 4% this year and 4.2% next, far above the global forecasts of 2.7% and many of the world's most rapidly growing economies – Ethiopia, Guinea, Rwanda, Uganda – are in Africa.



The 54 African nations are creating a $3.4 trillion single market, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), designed to pare back internal tariffs and nontariff barriers and lift intra-African trade from its current, disappointing, level of around 15% of total African trade.

Despite these encouraging developments the African agriculture picture is one of unfulfilled promise. According to UNCTAD, 794 million Africans – about 60% of the continent's population – experience food insecurity. Despite, an abundance of fertile land, over 80% of Africa's food is imported.

Cereal production has risen 37% over the past decade, but crop yields are only about 40% of the global average. This trend is unlikely to be arrested while prices for fertilizer continue to rise so dramatically. Nitrogen-based fertilizer prices have increased more than 30% since the outbreak of war in the Middle East while urea prices have jumped by 47% since the end of February.

African governments, the African Union and the African Development Bank are all keenly aware of this troubling situation. The problem is not a lack of will or even of resources. What is lacking is a global approach to the problem, one through which African governments, farmers, forest managers and fishers can develop programmes tailored to their specific strengths and needs. Each of the 54 African countries has different economic, political and social conditions. No single approach will adequately address the needs of all countries which is why it is important that every African country be empowered to develop its own programs, supported by partner institutions.

This is where the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) can play a pivotal role in improving agriculture policy in Africa and around the world. FAO is uniquely positioned to support such programmes by providing technical, political and strategic support. The FAO can draw on expertise and resources from its 193 member states while facilitating and enhancing co-ordination between African policymakers and international bodies like the World Bank, the European Union, the World Trade Organization and the United Nations.

If I am chosen to lead this important organization, one of my first priorities will be to de-centralize its operations, put more FAO boots on the ground in Africa and across the developing world where problems can be readily identified.

Enhancing food security must be at the heart of any action plan. A food insecurity rate of 60% is not acceptable. There can be no political or economic stability if people are hungry.

Many of the most important objectives on the African agricultural agenda – tackling food insecurity and hunger, sustainability, higher value-added production and job creation – are interconnected. Technology provides a common platform for achieving all these goals through improved productivity which raises incomes, creates jobs and fosters greater equity.

Technology also offers the best route for combating climate change. Volatile climate conditions represent a real threat to the livelihoods of African producers. As the world braces for another encounter with El Niño, the periodic weather pattern which brings drought and severe rains, African producers are highly vulnerable as are producers in Latin America. Markets already predict weather induced supply disruption. This is nothing new: in 1982-83 a very strong El Niño led to a 12% drop in cocoa production, while in 2023-24 the system's return depressed cocoa output by 13%.

It's not only crops that are threatened. Drought is endangering African forests as well. These forests provide livelihood for more than 500 million people and offer a vital source of carbon dioxide capture.

Promoting the use of solar power in African agriculture is one clear solution. Solar powered water pumps help farmers boost yields while slashing water consumption. In some cases, tech assisted producers have seen yields climb 32%, water usage drop 35% and spending on inputs fall 28%.

Spatial mapping can greatly enhance resource allocation and new and innovative processing techniques can cut energy consumption by 40% and water usage by 35%.

Business to business information platforms provide pricing and other market data to 45 million African farmers. Blockchain and Artificial Intelligence (AI) can assist farmers with their payments while enabling them to trace their products through all stages of the supply chain.

Better integration into global supply chains and lifting agriculture producers up the value-added ladder are also important goals of African governments. Ghana and the Ivory Coast produce 60% of the world's supply of raw cocoa but only about a third of Ghana's output is processed by domestic companies. In the Ivory Coast the figure is also less than 50%. In the $165 billion global chocolate industry, African producers take in only about 6% of the profits. It's the same story with coffee and tea produced in East Africa, fruits produced in Southern Africa and nuts, oilseeds and spices produced in Nigeria and Sudan.

By lifting value added production African governments help raise incomes and create more jobs – including for women who comprise most of the African agricultural workforce. Cassava processing is a good example. This $5.8 billion industry – in which companies produce high-quality flour, industrial starch and ethanol – directly employs approximately 3.2 million people while indirectly supporting another 8 million jobs. Women entrepreneurs lead 45% of small and medium-scale processing enterprises.

Here too technology plays a key role. In 2023, 35% of medium to large-scale processors implemented automated systems and digital solutions for supply chain management. Among those employing such techniques post-harvest losses have been reduced by 30%.

In Rwanda, AI-powered drone spraying and IoT-enabled irrigation – which can slash water consumption by 30%, by instantly assessing weather conditions and providing the precise amount of water required – and greenhouse tools are spreading across a sector that still employs 60% of the workforce, while digital services like the Smart Nkunganire System are streamlining input distribution.

In Kenya, drones have enabled farmers to cut pesticide use by up to 30% and water needs by 40%. Drones can cover ten acres an hour — ten times more than manual spraying — but only 5-7% of smallholders currently have access to the technology, a reminder of the equity gap still to close.

Innovation is also taking root in the continent's smaller, more climate-exposed economies: the Seychelles are piloting aquaponics systems that recycle fish waste to fertilise vegetables, easing pressure on its scarce land and water.

The lesson holds across East Africa as it does for the continent as a whole: technology, designed and deployed equitably and backed by patient investment, is what will finally convert agricultural potential into food security, jobs and resilience. Benefit must accrue to all stakeholders including smallholder farmers, women and youth.

Close 

Absent the required financial resources none of these efforts will get off the ground. Governments and international aid agencies can, and do, provide funds. The African Union's Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Programme (CAADP) supports farmers through a framework for the delivery of continent-wide technical and financial assistance. In 2025, the AU launched the CAADP Strategy and Action Plan to mobilize over the next decade $100 billion in financing.

Overall, 2022 investment in African agriculture came to $49 billion including public, private, and development financing. This may seem like a lot, but it works out to only about $140 per African farmer per year, versus an annual average of $1,300 for farmers globally. African farmers receive less than 3% of total global development funds and less than 4% of total investments in Africa from all sources combined.

Clearly, private sector partners must be mobilized. It's a big challenge but there are real investment opportunities on the horizon as the AfCFTA comes online, producers move into higher value products and technology increases yields while lowering costs. The FAO has a role here in bringing together investors and producers.

The world is changing profoundly and at an unprecedented pace. To meet the extraordinary challenges we face, the FAO must change too. The organization must focus political attention on food and nutrition security and its foundational role in global security. We must reform the traditional model of development cooperation to better address not only food and nutrition insecurity but climate variability, economic shocks, supply chain disruptions and rising inequality.

Above all, a new FAO for a new world means placing farmers, rural communities and countries at the very centre of everything it does.

Phil Hogan is former European Union Commissioner for agriculture. He is a candidate to become the next Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization.

World.title: Pumpkin spice invades summer as Americans kickstart fall traditions earlier than ever
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

If it seems like fall décor and seasonal food and drinks are arriving earlier each year, it's not just in your head.

Data show consumers are increasingly embracing "season creep" — shopping for seasonal products earlier than they did in years past.

Younger consumers' enthusiasm for fall, a desire to plan ahead and retailers' efforts to extend seasonal spending may all be helping drive the shift.

STARBUCKS TO PROMPT MORE TIPPING ON CARD PAYMENTS, FUELING 'TIP CREEP' BACKLASH

Last year, the popular pumpkin spice latte (PSL) returned to Dunkin' on Aug. 20 and to Starbucks on Aug. 26. Both coffeehouse chains brought their fall offerings back a day earlier this year, with Dunkin' launching its fall menu on Aug. 19 and Starbucks bringing back its PSL on Aug. 25, Florida Today reported.

Data from online grocery delivery and pickup service Instacart showed that in 2024, "the seasonal peak for orders containing pumpkin spice items occurred on September 17, a full 10 days earlier than in 2023."

Demand also cooled sooner, according to Instacart, though orders for pumpkin spice items, such as flavored coffee creamers and yogurts, spiked again in November as Thanksgiving drew near.

Food delivery service DoorDash reported in 2025 that "pumpkin spice is brewing sooner than ever."

CLICK HERE TO 

PSL demand spiked on Aug. 19, nearly two weeks earlier than in 2021, the company reported.

DoorDash also found that grocery orders for ingredients used to make fall-inspired drinks at home began spiking in late July.

According to the National Retail Federation (NRF), 49% of consumers said in 2025 that they would begin shopping for Halloween before October, compared with 34% a decade earlier.

"More 18- to 24-year-old early shoppers say they look forward to fall or that Halloween is one of their favorite holidays, and they plan accordingly," the NRF reported. "Their early Halloween shopping isn't about 'impulse purchases,' but rather intentional planning ahead."

Younger shoppers were much more likely to say they wanted to avoid the stress of last-minute shopping for décor and costumes, according to the NRF survey.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Seasons affect people's minds and behavior for several reasons, Michael Varnum, professor and social psychology area head at Arizona State University, told Fox News Digital.

Some of these effects are physiological, such as the ways our bodies and hormones respond to changes in light, temperature and other climatic conditions throughout the year, he said.

The way seasons cause changes in illness, travel or population may also cue changes in how we think and act, Varnum noted.

"How we respond to seasons isn't purely driven by actual changes in the environment but is also shaped by other associations, traditions, rituals and schedules – spring break, back to school in fall, Halloween, Christmas, etc. – that are built into our society and what we learn from an early age," he said.

Climate and the environment also likely play a part, he said, reasoning that hotter summers could make people more eager for the cooler weather of fall.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Varnum said it's interesting that our culture's comfort in and enjoyment of seasonal traditions are heavily shaped by a model of four seasons "that doesn't necessarily fit well with what actually changes in the weather and environment in all parts of the world."

He also acknowledged that a big part of season creep may be driven by marketing.

"My guess is that retailers and others hope to capture boosts in spending associated with holidays or seasonal shifts earlier with the idea that it might extend the period for which they'll see it in their sales," he said.

He added that it would be "interesting to know whether such marketing might be more or perhaps less effective when there is more of a mismatch between the season being invoked and the actual weather or time of year."

World.title: Dodgers and Braves offenses should have a field day with two questionable pitchers on the mound
World.content:
It was not a very fun day on the diamond for me. The bullpens got me in both games last night, and I went 0-2. It was a very frustrating thing to watch. Basically, picture yourself building a tower of cards or popsicle sticks only for someone to come and take away the foundation right as you're about to finish the job. The Cubs bullpen gave up five runs over the final two innings, losing the game. And Mason Miller, one of the best closers in baseball, allowed a run in a scoreless game to give the Pirates a win. Sometimes you can't dodge bad luck. Hopefully, I get some positive play in my favor now.

The Los Angeles Dodgers come into this one as just the second team in baseball to win 80 games. Although they will almost certainly win the National League West, they are still in a battle with the Brewers for the #1 overall seed in both the National League and the Majors. What is wild about the Dodgers is they aren't even playing with their best possible team. The pitching staff is finally looking a bit healthier than normal, but Will Smith is out, Kyle Tucker is playing poorly, Shohei Ohtani isn't pitching, and Dalton Rushing is also on the injured list. There is still another level the Dodgers can go to.

The roster might as well be an All-Star team, and this pitching staff is absurd. Tyler Glasnow is their fifth starter on the depth chart — he would be the first for probably about 25 other teams. Due to the injuries and conservation of the staff, the team throws a sixth starter, Roki Sasaki. He is one of the younger guys in the rotation, and someone who it seems like the Dodgers are still trying to figure out how to use. He was outstanding in the postseason for them last year. This season, in 22 starts, he is 5-5 with a 4.42 ERA and a 1.30 WHIP. He has pitched fairly well in August, but Braves hitters have been decent against him with three hits in just 11 at-bats.

The Atlanta Braves aren't too far behind the Dodgers, but they now must once again fend off the Phillies, who are hot on their tail. Two weeks ago, it felt like the Braves would coast to the postseason as the leaders in the National League East. Now they only have a 4.5-game lead, and most of that is due to the Phillies being hot, and less about the Braves struggling. However, over their last 10 games, the Phillies are 8-2, while the Braves are just 4-6. Still, the chances of either team missing the postseason are pretty low.

Looking to complete the series win over the Dodgers is AJ Smith-Shawver. For the season, Smith-Shawver has made only two starts, allowing six earned runs in 8.2 innings. He has walked five batters while giving up nine hits in that span as well, so there has been plenty of traffic on the base paths. This will be his first home start, and that could be a benefit to him as young guys might need that home crowd behind them. This is actually his fourth year in Major League time, so he has faced two Dodgers hitters and they are 2-for-7 against him. Alex Call is 2-for-5 with a double and triple.

It really doesn't mean much, but it would give Atlanta a little more confidence.
