World.title: Jelly Roll unleashes crude jokes about Trump's weight on 'Kimmel', 'from one fat pig to another'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Country music star Jelly Roll, who previously said he was not political, mocked President Donald Trump's weight, physical fitness and approval ratings Monday night in Los Angeles while guest-hosting "Jimmy Kimmel Live!", while using the president's appearance at Washington's Freedom 250 Grand Prix and recent physical as material for his opening monologue.

"Well, Mr. President, from one fat pig to another, take it from me that physical fitness is very important. And trust me, you’ll be happy to see your penis again," Jelly Roll said. "It’s crazy. Think about this, y’all. In the last few years, I’ve lost 300 pounds. That means I’ve lost an entire Donald Trump."

"And let’s be honest, based on his approval ratings, it seems like most of the country wants to do the same thing," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to the RNC for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

TRUMP TAKES HONORARY LAP AROUND INDYCAR TRACK IN WASHINGTON AHEAD OF FREEDOM 250 GRAND PRIX

A Reuters/Ipsos survey released last week placed Trump at 33% approval and 64% disapproval, tying the lowest approval rating across both of terms, Fox News Digital reported.

"President Trump has signed the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, driven violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital in response to questions about the polling.

"President Trump is cleaning up Joe Biden’s mess, and there is more work to do, but the United States of America has never been stronger," she continued.

Jelly Roll began the political portion of the monologue by discussing Sunday's Freedom 250 Grand Prix. Trump and first lady Melania Trump completed an honorary lap in the presidential limousine before the president waved the green flag to start the race, which Kyle Kirkwood won, according to OutKick.

TRUMP CALLS ON ALL FUTURE CANDIDATES TO TAKE COGNITIVE EXAM, NOTING PERFECT SCORE DURING LATEST PHYSICAL

"The president seemed to enjoy the IndyCar race, which was a real switch up for him, because normally he only likes his own race," Jelly Roll said.

He joked about the reaction to his previous Trump quips on Tuesday night's "Kimmel" show, saying he couldn't believe he would have "stunned" anyone with Trump jokes.

"Some folks online were upset that I didn't treat the president with reverence and dignity," he said. "But I want to remind ya'll that I go by the name Jelly Roll. I don't even treat myself with reverence and dignity."

He added the president should be able to "handle a few jokes."

"I get it that some people are mad at me for goofing on Trump, but if you wanted me to make jokes about Kamala Harris, you should have voted for her," he said.

TRUMP MARKS 80TH BIRTHDAY, NOW SECOND OCTOGENARIAN SITTING PRESIDENT: 'SEEMED TO UTTERLY DEFY AGE'

The monologue marked a rare political turn for Jelly Roll, whose real name is Jason DeFord. After the Grammy Awards in February, he declined to offer an immediate opinion about the country’s political climate and questioned why people would seek his views, Fox News Digital reported.

"You know, I’m a dumb redneck. Like, I haven’t watched enough. I didn’t have a phone for 18 months," Jelly Roll said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

His Monday remarks also differed from his response after meeting Trump at UFC 309 in 2024, when the then-president-elect told Jelly Roll that he liked his song "Save Me." Jelly Roll defended the encounter and said his family taught him to honor the office regardless of its occupant.

Jelly Roll first guest-hosted "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" in July 2025 and returned this week while Kimmel was on his summer break.

World.title: Green New Dodge: El-Sayed runs from policy as newly surfaced deleted posts show years of support
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed told Fox News host Jesse Watters on Monday that he would not defend the Green New Deal when confronted with his past support for the progressive climate proposal, a notable shift from years of publicly embracing it by name.

"Look, I’m not going to defend the Green New Deal," El-Sayed told Watters after the host confronted him over his past support for the proposal. When Watters reiterated that El-Sayed was on record supporting it, El-Sayed redirected the discussion toward lowering energy costs and creating Michigan jobs by prioritizing renewables.

Michigan, which Trump won in 2024 but lost in 2020, is shaping up to have one of the most competitive Senate races in the country, with the likely narrow results in the state potentially determining control of Congress. Critics charge that El-Sayed is downplaying some of his past beliefs and scrubbing his online footprint to appear more moderate, and therefore more palatable, to Michigan voters.

UNEARTHED CLIP EXPOSES MORE ANTI-POLICE RHETORIC AS EL-SAYED GETS GRILLED FOR DELETING SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

Though El-Sayed declined to defend the Green New Deal in front of a national audience, he previously hasn’t been so shy.

A Fox News Digital review of El-Sayed's deleted social media posts, preserved via the Internet Archive, uncovered dozens of examples of the Michigan Senate hopeful defending the Green New Deal by name.

"Rather than announcing the next iteration of this or that car at [the North American International Auto Show 2019], I’d love to see automakers announce that they support the #GreenNewDeal," El-Sayed wrote in January of that year.

On the primary campaign trail, Rep. Haley Stevens criticized El-Sayed over his past support for the Green New Deal on the grounds that it could lead to job losses in the automobile manufacturing industry.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS DEMOCRATS TURN LEFT, BLACK VOTERS TAP THE BRAKES

"The struggle for the Green New Deal uplifts the struggle for racial justice," El-Sayed wrote in April 2019.

The Green New Deal is a 2019 progressive policy framework floated by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Ed Markey that seeks to gradually transition the United States’ electrical grid away from fossil fuels. Their plan has become synonymous with the left-wing faction of the Democratic Party, leading many Democrats running in competitive races to distance themselves from it.

In another post, this time from September 2019, El-Sayed wrote "I believe in a Green New Deal" five times in all caps. He also suggested that the Green New Deal is essential to preserve freedom of speech because there can be no First Amendment "without the freedom to breathe the breath you have to take to speak in the first place."

"The #GreenNewDeal doesn’t center polar bears or glaciers, it centers those children forced to breath (sic.) in corporate pollution in their communities," El-Sayed wrote. "I stand with the Green New Deal because it stands for those kids."

WATCH: SURFACED VIDEOS OF DEM SENATE CANDIDATE BACKING 'DEFUND THE POLICE' CONTRADICT RECENT DENIALS

CNN previously reported that El-Sayed scrubbed large swathes of his commentary from the internet prior to announcing his run for Senate. The deletions appear to have been selective, as he still has some posts up from before he launched his campaign.

In his since-deleted social media posts, El-Sayed endorsed the "defund the police" movement, argued cities spent too much policing poverty and described police departments as "standing armies we deploy against our own people." In a separate YouTube video that was later hidden, he floated replacing the Second Amendment’s right to bear arms with a constitutional right to health care and called Border Patrol agents "white supremacists" while blaming American policies for migration from struggling nations.

Though El-Sayed regularly mentioned the Green New Deal on X prior to running for Senate, he has not posted the phrase even once since announcing his candidacy, a review found.

The El-Sayed campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

World.title: Federal judge strikes down Texas restriction on drag shows, offers people a 'simple' solution
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A federal judge in Texas struck down a state-level ban on drag shows Tuesday, saying the law violated the First Amendment.

The ruling from U.S. District Judge David Hittner, a Reagan appointee, prevents Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton from enforcing the ban and also rejects Paxton's request for a new trial on the case.

The Texas law, Texas Senate Bill 12, imposed up to a $10,000 fine on business owners for hosting drag show events. Performers at the events could have also been charged with a class A misdemeanor.

IOWA TEACHERS SUSPENDED OVER VIRAL STUDENT-RUN DRAG SHOW REACH SETTLEMENT BEFORE TRIAL

Hittner offered advice to supporters of the law and "those who find such activities as described in this case offensive."

"The solution is relatively simple ... just don’t go," he wrote.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

This is the second time Hittner has struck down the Texas law in a ruling. He did the same thing in 2023, but the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals handed the case back down with further instructions on how to decide the case.

The Texas law sought to justify its ban on the claim that drag shows appeal to "the prurient interest," but Hittner brushed that claim aside.

SEATTLE PRIDE PARADE PANDEMONIUM AS NUDE MARCHERS PRANCE THROUGH STREETS IN FRONT OF CHILDREN

"There are ‘erotic’ elements in countless popular performances that could be subject to both civil and criminal penalties under S.B. 12," he wrote, going on to list "cheerleading, dancing, live theater, and other common public occurrences," as activities that could be banned under the law.

Hittner also referenced Dolly Parton, saying her performances could easily have met the definition due to her being "a voluptuous sex symbol because of her big hair, flamboyant clothes and breast exposure."

GEORGIA PRIDE GROUP RECRUITING KIDS AS YOUNG AS 13 INTO DRAG SHOWS SPARKS BACKLASH

The ruling comes weeks after a federal appeals court approved a Florida law restricting children from sexually explicit performances, including many drag shows.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Florida law defines an "adult live performance" as a live show that "depicts or simulates nudity, sexual conduct, sexual excitement, or specific sexual activities ... lewd conduct, or the lewd exposure of prosthetic or imitation genitals or breasts" and that also predominantly appeals to a "prurient, shameful, or morbid interest," is "patently offensive" for the age of the child present and, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value for that child's age.

World.title: The ultimate dog-friendly road trip on Minnesota's North Shore from Duluth to Grand Marais
World.content:
A few weeks ago, I set out with the intention of writing an itinerary for the ultimate dog-friendly vacation on the Minnesota North Shore. Turns out, that's not as easy as I thought.

Not for a lack of writing material, either.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

No, the challenge I ran into was that I couldn't fit all the outdoor adventures the area had to offer into the measly three days I planned to visit.

Not a bad problem to have.

Every summer, my husband and I visit my mother-in-law at her snowbird summer home in Minocqua, Wisc. During that trip, we like to take a few days to drive up to Lake Superior and see what kind of hiking we can find. In 2024, we explored the Porcupine Mountains in Michigan's Upper Peninsula. Last year, it was the Apostle Islands at the tippy top of Wisconsin.

YOU DON'T NEED A KAYAK TO APPRECIATE NORTHERN WISCONSIN'S APOSTLE ISLANDS

This year, we figured we'd try Minnesota.

So I booked us a little Airbnb right on the lakeshore in Tofte, we threw our packs, our boots and our German Shepherd in the truck, and away we went.

Day 1: Iona's Beach & Split Rock Lighthouse

Admittedly, before this trip, I knew nothing about the stretch of land between Duluth and the Canadian border — aside from the fact that it's very cold in the wintertime, and I imagined every guy up there probably looked something like the Brawny Man. So I relied on my old friend Google (and my very helpful Nightcaps readers) to build our itinerary.

Did you know there are eight state parks in that 150 miles of shoreline? EIGHT. So I knew we, sadly, weren't going to hit them all on this trip. We'd have to pick a few and save the rest for next year.

At least a couple dozen people told me I had to go to Betty's Pies in Two Harbors — an iconic little café that's been around for 70 years. They have, I'm told, the best pies in all of Minnesota. Maybe all the Midwest. And like an idiot, I didn't listen.

Instead, our first stop was at Iona's Beach. Which was delightful, too.

Iona's Beach is a cute little crescent-shaped shore in Two Harbors that, instead of sand, is covered by salmon-colored pink rocks. In other words, this is not the sort of beach where you stroll barefoot. The stones are pink because they're made of rhyolite, a rock formed from ancient volcanic activity.

The area is named after a sweet little old lady named Iona Lind, whose family originally owned the land and ran the resort that used to stand where the parking lot is now.

Supposedly, the pebbles make a "singing" sound as Lake Superior's waves shift them back and forth against each other. But if I'm being honest, they just sounded like regular rocks to me.

Still, Iona's Beach is worth your time for a quick stroll and some photos along the shore.

Next up, we hit Split Rock Lighthouse.

A couple of things to note about Split Rock Lighthouse:

Dogs are allowed on the grounds but not inside the lighthouse itself. Because of this, we stayed outside.

To get the majestic, postcard view of the lighthouse from the bottom of the cliff, you have to pay for the $7 one-day vehicle permit to enter Split Rock State Park. There is a "View of the Lighthouse" scenic spot that you can pull into on US 61, but I promise you cannot see squat from there. Skip it and just pony up the $7.

After hitting the Tofte General Store beer-bait-barbecue-and-tackle shop (not what it's called, but it should be) for some food to cook, we headed to our Airbnb.

Friends, when I tell you it was like stepping back in time, I mean it. This particular property was built in the early 1970s and almost certainly has not been updated since. Our particular condo, though, had a 90s vibe — complete with an impressive collection of VHS tapes. We're talking "Liar Liar," "A Few Good Men," "Forrest Gump," "Titanic"! All the hits.

But we didn't choose this rental for the decor. We chose it because it's located smack on the top of a cliff overlooking Lake Superior. The kind of view that makes you want to pop open a bottle of wine, sit down in an Adirondack chair and just stare into the horizon.

And you best believe that's what I did.

Day 2: Palisade Head & Tettegouche State Park

We planned Wednesday to be our big hiking day. But first, a quick stop to check out the giant rock formation they call Palisade Head. It's a 300-foot granite cliff created in the Ice Age, and it's a seriously cool challenge for rock climbers.

Or you can take the easier route like we did. Park your car in the designated viewing area and admire Palisade Head from afar. While we were there, we made conversation with a couple of dudes who proceeded to list all the cool hiking spots we needed to check out during our trip to the North Shore. It was at this moment I realized I should have scheduled out more than three days.

HERE’S HOW TO DO THE SMOKY MOUNTAINS WITHOUT TRAFFIC AND CROWDS

From there we headed to Tettegouche State Park. I kept pronouncing it "Tet-uh-GOOCH-ee" (à la "way down yonder on the Chattahoochee.") However, a sign in the visitor center informed me the correct pronunciation is "TET-uh-goosh."

Bummer.

There are roughly 23 miles of hiking trails in Tettegouche, so we hopped on AllTrails and created our own adventure: Shovel Point to High Falls to Two Step Falls. I think we made the right choice.

Our route took us out to the lake shore, down along the river, to an incredible swimming hole at the base of High Falls, through some woody terrain and into a peaceful little lunch spot on the stream at Two Step. It worked out to about 6.2 moderate miles with multiple spots for Rocky to hop in the water and cool off.

High Falls was the star of the show.

On our way back to the condo, we decided to drive up Oberg Mountain. The loop gave us stunning vistas and a really cool overlook of Oberg Lake. I was pretty tired after Tettegouche, but this was well worth the extra 2.5 miles.

That night we headed up to Moguls Grill & Taproom for post-hike burgers and beers. It's inside the Caribou Highlands Lodge, which serves as a ski resort in the wintertime. Dogs aren't allowed inside the restaurant, but we snagged some food to go and sat out on the patio.

There, we met a nice elderly lady named Patrice who said she comes to the North Shore a few times a year "to escape the far-left hell scape of Minneapolis."

Day 3: Pincushion Mountain, Grand Marais & Cascade River State Park

Those fellas up on Palisade Head told us we have to check out the Gunflint Trail.

So much great hiking on the Gunflint Trail! Beautiful country! Such cool wildlife! I see moose all the time!

I do not love the idea of running into a grumpy moose out on the trail. But their sales pitch got me.

Upon further research, though, I discovered the Gunflint Trail is actually a 57-mile byway that stretches all the way from the lakeshore into the Boundary Waters and damn near to Canada. Since we didn't budget enough time to cover all that ground, we chose the very first trail off the Gunflint: Pincushion Mountain.

On the way up US 61, though, we stopped at a local coffee shop called Fika that came highly recommended by our Airbnb host.

Holy cow, you guys, are you familiar with maple syrup lattes? Because they are, I learned, very much a thing in northern Minnesota.

Now listen, I drink my coffee like my grandpa does: strong, black and by the bucket. One step short of jet fuel. But what's the point of driving 16 hours from home if you don't try the local fare?

My goodness. That maple syrup latte was worth every bit of the (probably) 500 calories it cost me. What a concept. Consider it fuel for the 5.75-mile Pincushion Mountain Loop.

Half of this trail was on an old logging road, which the curmudgeonly reviewers on AllTrails didn't love. I swear people on AllTrails will complain about everything.

The grass was too tall in some places. I had to step over a log. A bug landed on my shoulder!

You're in the woods, Sharon.

That said, the logging road portion of this trail was a little boring, but that's fine. Because the payoff was an epic view of Lake Superior and Grand Marais from the top of a massive bald monolith.

Pro tip: Make sure you veer off this loop to check out Barrier Falls. We went down to the bridge at West Devil Track before turning around and heading back to the loop.

The climb out of there was a bit of a b----, but suck it up, buttercup. You've got a maple syrup latte to burn off.

After this hike, we walked around Grand Marais — a charming little harbor town. We stopped by the Gunflint Tavern for lunch. But heads up, it is not dog friendly except for the upstairs bar, which does not serve food. It does, however, serve the Fulton 300 IPA, which is 10/10 if you're into that sort of thing.

If you find yourself in Grand Marais, do yourself a favor and make the windy walk out to the lighthouse. I can't believe I'm saying this, but it was so cold out there that I cursed myself for not bringing a beanie. In July!

Grand Marais is just about 35 miles to the Canadian border. However, my husband and I did not go to Canada. Because we are PATRIOTS.

Just kidding. It's because both of our passports are expired. But we plan to remedy that soon.

On our way out of town, we noticed Voyageur Brewing Company. It looked like a fun spot, and I wish we would have known about it ahead of time. They have a blonde ale that's very popular around these parts.

One cool thing about the North Shore is that everything is right off US 61. You really can't get lost. So on our way back to Tofte, we stopped for a quick 1-miler at Cascade River State Park.

This is an easy little trek — even after you enjoyed a beer or three in Grand Marais. Ask me how I know.

The Minnesota North Shore surpassed our expectations

The next morning, I set my alarm for 5 a.m. so that I could catch the sunrise. With a perfectly east-facing condo right on Lake Superior, it'd be criminal if I didn't drag my butt up for one sunrise.

And, friends, it was so, so worth it.

On our way back to Minocqua, we popped in Coho Cafe & Bakery. No exaggeration — the best pancakes I'd ever tasted in my life. Absolute perfection.

As we enjoyed our breakfast, we plotted next year's adventure. Grand Portage, Thunder Bay, Devil's Kettle, the Summit Express gondola up Lutsen Mountain, the Boundary Waters. All the things we just didn't have time for this year. And all dog friendly.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Truthfully, we fell in love with Grand Marais. That seems like an obvious base camp for the 2027 Great White North adventure.

And I promise — this time — we're hitting Betty's Pies.

World.title: Seven-year-old boy forced to hike Mt. Fuji alone after dad, older brother abandon him
World.content:
Hiking is often viewed as a strenuous activity that only the most seasoned athletes can partake in, but the truth of the matter is that it's actually for everyone.

Even families can enjoy hiking as long as they come prepared and stay together.

The latter part of that equation was apparently too much to ask for a father and his two sons last Thursday while hiking the famous Mt. Fuji in Japan.

According to an ABC news affiliate in North Carolina, at around 7:40 am local time, a mountain hut worker reportedly saw a 7-year-old boy sitting on a bench and looking exhausted.

The worker then contacted the police, who subsequently contacted the boy's father to try and reunite the two parties.

As it turns out, the younger boy was hiking the mountain with his father and older brother when he complained of feeling tired.

Instead of turning around and heading home or taking a break with his son, the father told him to "wait here" and then continued on ahead with his older son in tow.

The father left his son at a station around 8,000 feet above sea level as fog and rain reportedly started to roll in, making it dangerous for anyone to be alone, much less a 7-year-old boy.

When local police reunited the boy with his other family members, they admonished the father for endangering the child.

The inclement weather conditions and fatigue combined with the altitude sickness that could set in at that height are a bad combination for even the most experienced hikers.

The father reportedly told the police officers, "I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it."

Luckily, the boy was returned to his father unharmed.

As a father, I get a little nervous leaving my son in front of the TV for 20 seconds to go grab the laundry out of the dryer, so I couldn't imagine telling my young child to chill on the side of a mountain while I finish my hike.

I'm not trying to pile on the dad, as he sounds contrite, but maybe table the hike so your son doesn't get frostbite while you cosplay as Alex Honnold.

Let this be a lesson to all of you amateur hikers: always use the buddy system.

World.title: Trump-backed Mike Mazzei wins the GOP nomination in the Oklahoma governor’s race
World.content:
Former state Sen. Mike Mazzei has secured the Republican nomination for governor in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, a victory for President Donald Trump’s preferred candidate.

Mazzei narrowly defeated state Attorney General Gentner Drummond by about 2,000 votes in the GOP primary runoff.

The initial June primary was also tight. Drummond finished in first place by just more than 1,000 votes over Mazzei. Since no candidate in the crowded field secured a majority, the race went to a runoff.

In the weeks leading up to the runoff, Drummond outraised and outspent Mazzei, with his campaign reporting last week that he brought in $2.3 million between the mid-June primary and Tuesday’s runoff. Mazzei, in the same time period, raised $816,000.

Both candidates have also loaned their campaigns significant sums: $11 million for Mazzei and $3 million for Drummond.

Trump first endorsed Mazzei in May in the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Kevin Stitt and continued to reiterate his support for the former state lawmaker.

Mike Mazzei in Oklahoma City on April 8, 2026. Bryan Terry / USA Today Network via Reuters Connect

In a post on Truth Social last week, Trump praised Mazzei and criticized Drummond, writing, “Drummond is not the right guy. He’s got a bad attitude, and he doesn’t stand for the Values of Oklahoma, which must VOTE FOR ‘MIKE MAZZEI FOR GOVERNOR,’ on Tuesday, August 25th.”

Drummond also drew the president’s ire for suing to block the construction of the largest aluminum smelter in the country in Inola, Oklahoma, citing environmental and public health concerns.

“He wants to dethrone a magnificent, Job producing, desperately needed, and brand new, Aluminum Plant that will be one of the best projects ever conceived or built, not only in the Great State of Oklahoma, but in the United States, itself,” Trump wrote in the Truth Social post earlier this month.

Mazzei, on the other hand, supports construction of the plant.

This week, Drummond also broke with the president on his decision last week to waive tariffs on some beef imports in an attempt to lower beef prices in the U.S.

“I think Oklahoma and I are supportive of President Trump and many of his policies. I do think the majority of Oklahomans would agree that the tariffs are too far, that importing cheap beef only injures Oklahoma’s cattlemen, ranchers and farmers,” Drummond told NewsNation, echoing the concerns of GOP lawmakers in the House and Senate from states with large cattle-ranching communities.

While Trump’s endorsement remains the most coveted in GOP politics, he has had some stumbles, particularly in governor’s races. Five gubernatorial candidates he has backed this year failed to win their primaries.

With his victory Tuesday, Mazzei is the heavy favorite to win November’s general election, given the state’s deeply Republican voter base. He’ll face Democratic state Rep. Cyndi Munson in the general election.

World.title: Democratic socialists notch another win in the Oklahoma Senate primary runoff
World.content:
Nurse N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas has won the Democratic Senate primary runoff in Oklahoma, NBC News projects, securing another win for the party’s democratic socialist wing.

Thomas, a 31-year-old member of the Chickasaw Nation, defeated attorney and minister Jim Priest, 70, in the contest, despite being drastically outspent. The two advanced to a runoff after neither clinched a majority of the vote in the initial June primary.

Thomas will face GOP Rep. Kevin Hern, who will be heavily favored this fall to win the open seat to replace former Sen. Markwayne Mullin, now the secretary of homeland security. Oklahoma is a solidly Republican state that President Donald Trump won by 34 points in 2024.

Thomas’ primary victory comes as progressive candidates have made inroads across the country this year. Democratic socialists have won a handful of high-profile primaries in recent weeks, including in Florida’s Senate race and a key House battleground in Michigan.

Thomas is “a self-proclaimed democratic socialist,” she told NBC News in an interview Tuesday morning, though she said she is “not yet” a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. She described democratic socialists as “the next generation” that is “looking to change the system.”

Thomas said that she does not support every plank of the DSA platform. A military spouse, Thomas said she does not support defunding the Defense Department. She did voice support for a slew of progressive policies, including Medicare for All, universal childcare and parental leave, and “making sure that everyone pays their fair share.” Thomas said she also favors abolishing the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.

“The system right now doesn’t work for us and it never has,” said Thomas, noting her pitch to voters is focused on healthcare, as rural areas in the state are struggling with access to quality care.

Asked if she considered herself a capitalist or a socialist, Thomas said, “Capitalism is what’s destroying our country right now,” but she later described capitalism as “inevitable,” saying she supports the concept of people owning their own businesses and property.

Thomas said fellow democratic socialists were finding success in some primaries this year as voters are clamoring for change and “people-first” and “family-first” policies.

“I’m just ready for change and I think everyone else is as well,” she said.

Like some other progressive candidates who have prevailed in primaries this year, Thomas was outspent in the primary by a more moderate opponent.

Priest’s campaign has spent $315,000 so far, while Thomas’ campaign has spent $57,000, according to campaign finance reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. She is also starting the general election at a massive financial disadvantage: Thomas had just $456 in her campaign account as of Aug. 5, while Hern’s campaign had $2.6 million on hand as of June 30.

World.title: The second Dan Sullivan makes the general election in Alaska’s Senate race
World.content:
Former teacher Dan J. Sullivan will join Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola on the general election ballot in Alaska’s Senate race, NBC News projects.

Republicans have criticized the other Sullivan’s candidacy as a potential ploy to confuse voters in a key battleground race, which he has denied. Alaska’s election system might also blunt the impact of any confusion. The top four candidates, regardless of party, advance from Alaska’s all-party primary to a ranked-choice general election, meaning voters could rank both Sullivans.

But some voters end up ranking only one candidate, which could matter in a close race — and Alaska’s Senate race could be one of the closest in the country this year.

Democrats have targeted Alaska as an opportunity to flip a seat since well before the same-name saga consumed the race, even though President Donald Trump carried the state by double digits in each of the last three presidential elections.

Peltola, a former state legislator and city council member, became the first Alaska Native to represent the state in Congress when she won a statewide special election in 2022 and then a full term months later. Peltola lost her seat after one term by 3 percentage points, running well ahead of Vice President Kamala Harris at the top of the Democratic ticket in 2024.

Former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. Ellen Schmidt / Las Vegas Review-Journal via Getty Images file

Sullivan was first elected to the Senate in 2014, defeating a Democratic incumbent, and re-elected in 2020. A former Marine, he has touted his work for veterans and the state’s fishing industry.

His campaign and Republican allies have criticized the other Sullivan as a potential Democratic plant, noting that he only recently registered as a Republican and got help with his campaign launch from a Democratic consultant.

State and federal prosecutors are investigating whether his candidacy is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. The federal investigation is moving forward, with a law enforcement official telling NBC News that a grand jury issued subpoenas last week to compel information from witnesses related to the Dan J. Sullivan campaign.

The candidate told The New York Times that he registered as a Republican because his previous political party, the Alaska Independence Party, no longer exists. He declined to detail his involvement with the Democratic consultant because of the ongoing investigation.

World.title: Scores killed, Americans among hundreds missing after Nepal flash floods
World.content:
At least 95 people were killed and more than 400 listed as missing Wednesday in Nepal after flash flooding tore through valleys in the Himalayan country's northern border areas, according to authorities. Dozens of U.S. nationals were among the 341 foreigners listed as missing, according to Nepal's Tourism Board, citing information from tour companies.

The flash floods decimated villages, slamming into houses, roads, bridges and power plants. Videos broadcast by regional news outlets and posted on social media show violent torrents of water surging through valleys and mountain passes, tearing down bridges and dams and sweeping away buildings.

The Nepali prime minister's office confirmed that at least 95 people were killed, but there was no word on the nationalities of the victims.

Hikmat Singh Ayer, CEO and senior director of Nepal's Tourism Board, told CBS News that there were 403 people unaccounted for after the flooding. He said that 341 foreign nationals were missing, including 33 Americans, 34 Australians, 24 Canadians, 4 Germans, 19 Malaysians and one Israeli.

Residents look at houses partially submerged in muddy water after flash floods at Trishuli Bazar, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Aug. 26, 2026. Prakash MATHEMA/AFP/Getty

A sudden surge of water Wednesday morning in the Bhote Koshi River, in the country's northern Rasuwa district north of capital Kathmandu, quickly affected the neighboring Nuwakot and Dhading districts.

Nepali President Ramachandra Paudel said he was "extremely saddened" by the "loss of lives and property caused by the sudden flood."

He called on the government, political parties, agencies and the general public to intensify rescue and relief efforts.

"There could be heavy casualties or loss of property," district administrator Narendra Pariyar was quoted as saying by Reuters. He has also urged people living along the banks of the Bhote Koshi River to move to higher ground.

A screen grab captured from a video shared on social media by the Nepal Police shows a flash flood crashing through a valley near the Nepal-China border in Nepal, Aug. 26, 2026. Nepal Police/Handout/Anadolu via Getty

Nepal's mountainous terrain, dotted with deep valleys and narrow gorges, makes rescue and relief operations challenging. Helicopters could not land in the affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure, Reuters said.

Most of the missing foreigners were on trips organized by tourism and travel companies.

Houses lie partially submerged in mud and water along a river after flash floods at Trishuli Bazar, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Aug. 26, 2026. Prabin RANABHAT/AFP/Getty

The flash flood was caused by an earthquake that triggered a large landslide, which blocked the Bhote Koshi River, according to Nepal's Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal.

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) confirmed that six of its major hydropower and transmission facilities were damaged in the flooding.

"We do not exactly know the extent of damage, but the flood is big, and it could have damaged many settlements," Nepal Police spokesman Abi Narayan Kafle told the French news agency AFP. "We have alerted people who are staying near the riverside to relocate ... and deployed all our resources."

People look at destruction caused by flash floods and mudslides on the Nepal-China border, Aug. 26, 2026, in Nuwakot, Nepal. Safal Prakash Shrestha/Anadolu/Getty

"Work has started to take necessary steps in coordination with the medical team, scouts, and Red Cross," Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah wrote in a social media post.

India's government ordered authorities in states along the Nepal border to be on high alert.

World.title: Carly Pearce recalls meeting Dolly Parton at 16: "I couldn't believe she was real"
World.content:
Many country singers have shared their remembrances of meeting Dolly Parton after they became stars. But few were actually working at Dollywood when they met the legend.

Country star Carly Pearce met Parton when she was just 16 and performing as part of Dollywood's Country Crossroads show.

"I remember just staring at her because I couldn't believe she was real," Pearce told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday.

"She's exactly what everybody wants her to be in real life," she added.

Parton, whose groundbreaking career spanned six decades, 10 Grammy Awards and millions of fans, died at a Nashville, Tennessee, hospital on Tuesday after a brief battle with cancer, her team said in a statement. She was 80 years old.

Pearce had been part of a special show honoring Parton for her songwriting with the ACM Poet's Award last Wednesday. Parton recorded a video message for the show, thanking the Academy of Country Music for the award, saying, "Songwriting has always been the most important part of who I am creatively."

"I never thought of a world where she wouldn't be here," Pearce said Wednesday. "It just feels not real to me. I was so saddened. We had just honored her at the ACM Honors this past week. I sang '9 to 5' for her, and she had a little video and was a whole part of our show as the ACM icon. So it was just a really crazy thing."

Carly Pearce attends the ACM Honors at The Pinnacle on Aug. 19, 2026, in Nashville, Tennessee. Terry Wyatt/Getty Images for ACM

Parton was also wildly successful as a businesswoman, even though she was often underestimated in a financial world led by men. She owned the publishing rights to all of her music, which generated millions of dollars. In fact, Whitney Houston's massively popular recording of "I Will Always Love You" benefited Parton to the tune of many millions alone.

Country singer Lauren Alaina told "CBS Mornings" she was lucky enough to pick Parton's brain about her business empire several times.

"I asked her her best advice for me, and she said, 'Never put the career first. Put God first, then your family, then the career.' And she said, 'It's really worked for me,'" Alaina said. "I remember being so in awe of her career. And it really was such an impactful thing for me."

Another success for Parton turned out to be the unheralded purchase of a local theme park in western Tennessee. Parton's purchase in the 1980s of the park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, turned into the highly successful Dollywood where Pearce would later work.

"What I find to be really inspiring is, you think about that she was 80, and for decades she continued to raise the bar," Pearce told "CBS Mornings." "Look at everything she's got going on right now — a musical, a new hotel in Nashville, her travel gas station in Tennessee. I mean, the woman never stopped. At 80. And you just go, 'There is something to be said for always pushing and never thinking that you've quote-unquote made it.'"

World.title: 24 states sue to block new Postal Service rules for mail voting
World.content:
Washington — A coalition of 24 states and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit Wednesday that seeks to block a new rule from the U.S. Postal Service that imposes requirements for mail voting ahead of the November midterm elections.

The final rule, published by the agency last Friday, came in response to an executive order President Trump signed in March that seeks to tighten the rules for mail voting. The states argue in their lawsuit, filed in federal court in Massachusetts, that the rule will prevent them from administering their mail voting programs for the midterm elections and risks disenfranchising voters who cast their ballots by mail.

They said in their lawsuit that the Postal Service's new measure unconstitutionally exceeds the executive branch's power and interferes with states' authority to administer elections under their own laws.

"The Rule violates the Constitution and federal statutes many times over," the state attorneys general said. "It displaces state laws adopted pursuant to each State's constitutional authority to administer elections, erects new USPS functions and ballot mail constraints that are inconsistent with USPS's governing statutes, flouts USPS's procedural requirements, violates the Privacy Act, and cannot be reconciled with federal voting rights law."

They continued: "Each of these defects would alone establish the Rule's unlawfulness. Together, they demonstrate USPS's utter disregard for the law in carrying out the President's policy preferences."

The states warned that if the Postal Service's new requirements are allowed to take effect, election officials will have to devote time, money and resources to implement the changes.

The new measure from the Postal Service implements the plans laid out in Mr. Trump's executive order, which he said are necessary to protect the integrity of U.S. elections. The rule lays out design elements required for mail ballot envelopes, including trackable barcodes, and directs state election officials to submit to an online portal the names and addresses of voters to whom they intend to send mail ballots.

Voters will then be enrolled in a state-specific "Mail-In and Absentee Participation List," which the Postal Service said is "primarily intended to assist election officials and law enforcement to understand who may have been mailed a ballot, in order to identify potentially anomalous incidents that may merit further investigation."

The Postal Service "will not play any role in determining voter eligibility, maintaining voter rolls, or counting ballots," it said.

But the states said that as a result of the rule, they must immediately redesign their mail ballot envelopes to comply with its requirements and seek review from the Postal Service "at significant costs."

"Plaintiff States' election officials must also develop new systems at breakneck speed to convey mail voter lists to USPS to ensure that every eligible voter who is entitled to a mail ballot receives one, create new guidance for and train election officials, and educate the public about changes to mail voting," they said in the suit.

They warned that there may also be an influx of voters who choose to cast their ballots in person instead of by mail because of the Postal Service's changes.

"In short, they must accomplish multiple Herculean tasks, each necessary to address the disruption caused by the Rule, in a matter of weeks, with limited resources," the states said.

Nearly all of the states that signed onto the new lawsuit filed an earlier challenge to Mr. Trump's executive order. A federal district court blocked the administration from implementing key provisions of the order, including the directives for the Postal Service. But the Supreme Court on Monday halted the lower court's injunction.

In a 6-3 decision that rested on procedural grounds, the high court's conservative majority said the states filed their lawsuit too soon and found the district court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Trump administration from trying to implement the executive order.

"The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful," the Supreme Court said in an unsigned decision. "On that score, time will tell."

On the heels of that decision, Democratic campaign committees have also moved to file new lawsuits challenging the Postal Service's rule.

World.title: Watch Live: Lindsay Clancy trial jury hears from final witness today
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy's murder trial in Massachusetts will wind down Wednesday with testimony from the prosecution's final rebuttal witness.

You can watch it live on CBS News Boston in the embedded video or on YouTube when court is in session.

Dr. Gregory Saathoff, a professor of emergency medicine and a forensic psychiatrist who has worked with the FBI, was back on the witness stand in Plymouth Superior Court. Once he's done testifying on Wednesday, jurors will be sent home and lawyers for both sides will go through the next steps in the trial. Closing arguments are expected on Thursday.

Dr. Gregory Saathoff in Plymouth Superior Court on August 25, 2026. Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool

Cross-examination of final witness

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington began his cross-examination by noting that Saathoff didn't interview Clancy until more than three years after the murders.

He went through Saathoff's resume line-by-line, saying he's "written a lot about terrorism" but not much about postpartum depression. Saathoff said he last treated a woman suffering from postpartum psychosis in the 1990s.

Reddington said Clancy was complaining of dark thoughts and homicidal ideation to doctors and others in her community.

"The homicidal ideation, as I understand, was just voiced to her husband and her mother," Saathoff replied.

"Just voiced? Is that like talking about the Red Sox?" Reddington said. "She's talking about homicidal ideation of her children."

Reddington also questioned Saathoff's testimony about crushed-up pills being found in a wine tumbler in Clancy's bedroom.

"So how do we know that that's even drugs or medications?" Reddington asked.

"It was Patrick Clancy's observation," Saathoff said.

There were heated moments as Reddington asked Saathoff about his efforts to interview Clancy as well as her mother.

"Do you think for one minute when you're trying to put her in jail for her life that she wants to talk to you?" Reddington said before the judge stopped him.

Dr. Gregory Saathoff testimony

Saathoff began his testimony Tuesday. He interviewed Clancy in May and June of this year and talked to her about the voice she said she heard that ordered her to kill the children. He said she told him the voice stopped once the killings had ended. Saathoff also said there were inconsistencies in Clancy's story.

When Saathoff was back on the stand Wednesday, prosecutor Jennifer Sprague asked if the voice Clancy heard told her where or how to kill the children and herself. He said it was significant that it did not.

"It indicated that she had control," he said.

Saathoff characterized Clancy's suicide attempt as "very serious," even though prosecutors have previously highlighted that the cuts she inflicted on herself were not too severe.

"The fact that the lacerations were not deep doesn't mean that she wasn't intending to kill herself," he said.

Sprague asked Saathoff if Clancy was overmedicated, which is one of the defense's key arguments.

"She experienced some significant side effects from some of her medication," he said, but added she still had an ability to appreciate right from wrong.

Saathoff said it's his medical opinion that Clancy was criminally responsible for the murders, saying there was a significant amount of planning involved in sending Patrick Clancy to CVS and pick up takeout food, as well as choosing the basement and exercise bands for the murders.

"I believe that she expected to die and that by the time that Mr. Clancy arrived she would have successfully been able to take her life," he said.

Lindsay Clancy trial

Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the strangulation deaths of her children - 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan - in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023.

Clancy admits to killing her children. Her attorney said she should not be held criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said Clancy was not psychotic and planned the murders.

The jury of 12 women and six men have heard testimony from 85 witnesses since July 27.

If Clancy is convicted of first-degree murder, she faces life in prison without parole. If the jury determines she was not criminally responsible, she will be sent to a state psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts.

Lindsay Clancy in Plymouth Superior Court on August 25, 2026. Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental healthcare resources and support, the National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: Tim Curry, star of "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," dies at 80
World.content:
Actor Tim Curry, known for his iconic performances in cult classics like "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" and the original screen adaptation of Stephen King's "It," has died, his manager confirmed. He was 80.

Born in Cheshire, England, in 1946, the British singer and actor began his career on London's West End. He went on to receive multiple Emmy, Grammy and Tony awards, alongside additional acclaim, throughout his decades in the business.

Curry was best known for his portrayal of cross-dressing scientist Dr. Frank-N-Furter in "Rocky Horror," the 1975 musical comedy movie in which he starred alongside the likes of Susan Sarandon and Barry Bostwick. He reprised the role for the screen after first playing it in the stage musical "The Rocky Horror Show."

He's also remembered widely for his role in "It," in which he played the villainous clown Pennywise, when King's 1986 novel was adapted into a miniseries in 1990.

This is a breaking news story. Check back for updates.

World.title: Meta settles social media addiction suit for up to $17.1 billion
World.content:
Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, settled a landmark social media addiction lawsuit on Wednesday brought by dozens of states, according to a court filing.

Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to the states that sued and add child-safety measures to its platforms. The settlement resolves claims filed by 47 states and cuts short a trial that kicked off last week in Oakland, California.

California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among the 29 states that first filed suit against Meta in 2023, alleging that the technology giant used its social media platforms to "entice, engage and ultimately ensnare" young internet users. States accused Meta of deliberately designing its platforms to be addictive and of misleading users and the public about the risks.

Meta also violated the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) by collecting and using the personal data of residents under 13, the states alleged. Meta denied the claims.

In a statement on Wednesday, Meta called the settlement an important step and encouraged other social media players to implement safety measures to protect youth.

"We just announced an agreement with a bipartisan group of 52 Attorneys General across U.S. states, territories and the District of Columbia to set a new industry standard, building on our longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens," a Meta spokesperson said in an email. "While this is an important step, these protections will only be truly effective if our peers-TikTok and YouTube-put the same measures in place."

The $17.1 billion settlement, which remains subject to court approval, amounts to a fraction of Meta's 2025 revenue of $201 billion.

As part of the settlement, Meta will pay at least $12.1 billion over the next 10 years to the coalition states that sued and an additional $5 billion if other social media companies, including YouTube and TikTok, agree to settlements in the future, state attorneys general said.

A Meta spokesperson said the company settled separately with Texas, which was not part of the multistate settlement, bringing their total payout to approximately $18 billion.

Will new safeguards help?

Meta will put in place new child safety measures under the settlement, including a two-hour daily time limit for teens; a restriction barring minors from accessing Facebook and Instagram at night; and muted push notifications during school hours.

Meta will also enact changes to better verify the ages of its users who are under 18 and implement stronger, more user-friendly parental controls and limits on social-comparison features, such as "like" counts.

Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, where Meta is based, said the settlement will force the company to overhaul its approach to designing and operating social media.

"Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms — and will do it within months," he said in a statement. "We are talking about time limits, stopping notifications during school, a block on the app during critical overnight hours, bans on plastic surgery filters, and so much more."

As tech companies have faced growing pressure about the impact of social media in recent years, Meta has added a number of safety features to Instagram, including separate accounts for teenagers with stronger protections around messaging and privacy, along with content restrictions.

But some child safety experts and former Meta employees contend that such features are largely ineffective.

Arturo Béjar, a former Meta engineering director, said during his testimony in the trial last week that the company designed its social media platforms to keep people engaged even if it harmed their mental health.

"If you step away from the product, they are not going to make any money," he said.

The financial settlement will help states provide mental health services for young people and educate the public on the potential harm of social media, according to New York Attorney General Letitia James.

"With significant new resources for our communities and comprehensive restrictions on Meta's platforms for young people, we are taking a major step towards breaking the cycle of social media addiction," she said in a statement.
