Verduzco’s civil service career

Verduzco served as head of the high-performance program at the Sinaloa Institute of Physical Culture and Sport, a state government institute, during the governorship of Rubén Rocha Moya, who is also accused of drug trafficking by U.S. prosecutors. He left that position on July 31, according to the newspaper Milenio.

Verduzco previously served as the director of the Municipal Institute of Sport in Guasave, a city in Sinaloa around 150 kilometers northwest of the state capital, Culiacán. He occupied that position between 2022 and 2024. Before taking up that role, Verduzco was a manager with the Guasave water authority.

With reports from Milenio and Reforma

World.title: Brazil Posts Deeper IPCA-15 Deflation as Itaipú Bonus Cuts Power Bills
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Headline reading IPCA-15 fell 0.40% in August 2026, versus a 0.31% consensus decline

— Main driver Electricity fell 6.25%, the biggest drop since January 2025, on the Itaipú bonus

— Bonus size R$872 million (about US$170 million) approved by power regulator Aneel

— Market reaction DI futures for January 2029 slipped to 14.045% from 14.095%

— 12-month rate 4.24%, still above the 3% target center

The IBGE’s mid-month price gauge fell 0.40% in August, more than the 0.31% decline economists expected, as a US$170 million Itaipú credit cut electricity bills and pulled interest-rate futures lower.

Brazil’s mid-month inflation reading came in with deeper deflation than markets expected on Wednesday, 26 August 2026, sending interest-rate futures lower in São Paulo trading. The IPCA-15, the preview of the country’s official consumer price index, fell 0.40% in August, the statistics agency IBGE said, against a median forecast of a 0.31% decline compiled by Valor Data. The IPCA-15 deflation was the first negative monthly reading of 2026.

The Itaipú hydroelectric dam; its R$872 million bonus cut August electricity bills. Photo: Rio Times

IPCA-15 deflation comes in below the consensus

The 0.40% decline in the IPCA-15 deflation was steeper than the 0.31% drop most economists expected, according to the median of forecasts collected by Valor Data. In the 12 months through mid-August, the index rose 4.24%, the IBGE said. The mid-month gauge, which collects prices from mid-July to mid-August, previews the official IPCA due in September.

The reading follows a 0.06% increase in July and marks the first monthly deflation of the year, according to Estado de S. Paulo. The IPCA-15 deflation was concentrated in administered and volatile items, particularly electricity, food at home and airfares, while some services continued to rise.

The IPCA-15 tracks prices for families earning between one and 40 minimum wages across 11 urban areas of Brazil and uses the same methodology as the official IPCA, differing only in the collection window, which is brought forward by about two weeks. Because it lands before the full-month figure, it is the freshest inflation signal available to the central bank and typically moves rate markets on the day of release.

Itaipú bonus drives biggest power-bill drop since January 2025

Residential electricity prices fell 6.25% in the period, the largest decline since January 2025, when they dropped 15.46% for the same reason, Valor reported. The item knocked 0.26 percentage point off the monthly index, making it the single largest downward contribution.

The driver was the Itaipú bonus, a credit that returns to consumers part of the surplus from the energy commercialization account of the binational Itaipú hydroelectric dam. Power regulator Aneel approved the distribution of R$872 million, roughly US$170 million at current exchange rates, applied to bills issued between 1 and 31 August. The credit goes to residential consumers who had at least one month last year with consumption below 350 kWh.

The bonus more than offset upward pressure elsewhere in the electricity item. The yellow tariff flag remains in force in August, adding R$1.885 per 100 kWh consumed, and the period captured tariff increases of 19.55% in Curitiba, 14.89% for one utility in Porto Alegre and 8.85% for one utility in São Paulo, according to Valor. The IBGE has signaled the effect is temporary: without the one-off credit, the electricity item is expected to rebound in September even in the absence of new adjustments.

Rate futures slide after the IPCA-15 deflation

Interest-rate futures opened lower after the data. Around 9:10 a.m. local time, the DI contract for January 2027 slipped to 13.66% from 13.675%, the January 2028 contract fell to 13.765% from 13.815%, January 2029 eased to 14.045% from 14.095%, and January 2031 dropped to 14.295% from 14.35%, according to Valor. An additional 2% drop in oil prices on Wednesday morning also supported domestic fixed income.

The IPCA-15 deflation landed as markets assess the pace of monetary easing. The central bank reduced the Selic to 14.00% at its August meeting, and a softer inflation path would strengthen the case for further cuts, although the 12-month rate of 4.24% remains above the 3% target center, which carries a tolerance band of 1.5 percentage points in either direction. Traders were also awaiting July PCE inflation data in the United States, the Federal Reserve’s preferred gauge.

Falling food and transport costs broaden the disinflation

Beyond electricity, the August reading showed broad-based relief. The housing group fell 1.41%, the steepest decline among the index’s groups, pulled down by power bills. Transportation dropped 1.0%, reversing a 0.11% increase in July, as airfares plunged 13.3% and fuels fell 1.43%. Within fuels, ethanol fell 3.63%, gasoline 1.23% and diesel 0.71%, while vehicular natural gas rose 1.42%, the IBGE said.

Food and beverages declined 0.57%, a second consecutive month of deflation for the group, according to Valor, with food consumed at home down a sharper 0.97%, led by tomatoes, which fell 27.38%, and potatoes, down 25.14%. On the upside, personal expenses rose 0.66%, driven by cigarettes, and education increased 0.46%.

Economists caution that the composition of the August number matters as much as the headline. The electricity credit will drop out of the comparison base in September, and services inflation, which tends to track wages and a still-tight labor market, remains the component the central bank watches most closely. The full-month IPCA for August, due in September, will show whether the disinflation extends beyond the one-off utility credit.

Valor reports government doubled financial spending to sidestep fiscal framework

The benign inflation print contrasted with a separate report in Valor on Wednesday detailing how President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s government has worked around the fiscal framework it enacted in 2023. According to the newspaper, the government raised financial expenditure, which sits outside the framework’s limits on primary spending, from 0.9% of GDP in 2023 to 2.1% of GDP in 2026, mostly through credit stimulus measures.

The framework, known as the arcabouço, caps real growth in primary spending at between 0.6% and 2.5% a year, tied to revenue performance, and sets primary result targets. Because financial spending is excluded from those constraints, expanding it allows the administration to stimulate the economy without breaching the rule on paper.

Lívio Ribeiro, a researcher at FGV Ibre and a partner at consultancy BRCG, told Valor the measures create a hidden side to fiscal stimulus that makes it harder and more opaque to track the government’s impact on the economy, and that they complicate the central bank’s efforts to contain inflation. The juxtaposition of a one-off IPCA-15 deflation and an expanding fiscal footprint helps explain why markets expect the easing cycle to remain cautious.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Brazil post an IPCA-15 deflation in August 2026? Mainly because of the Itaipú bonus, a one-off credit of R$872 million approved by regulator Aneel and applied to August power bills, which drove residential electricity prices down 6.25%. Deflation in food at home and falling airfares and fuel prices added to the decline. What is the Itaipú bonus? It is a credit that returns to consumers part of the surplus from the energy commercialization account of the binational Itaipú hydroelectric dam. It is credited directly on the bills of residential consumers who had at least one month in the previous year with consumption below 350 kWh. How did markets react to the IPCA-15 deflation? Interest-rate futures fell after the deeper-than-expected reading. The DI contract for January 2029 eased to 14.045% from 14.095%, and shorter maturities also declined, as traders weighed a faster pace of Selic cuts from the current 14.00%.

World.title: Two Workers Killed in YPF Vaca Muerta Accident at Rincón del Mangrullo
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Argentina · ENERGY

Key Facts — Location Rincón del Mangrullo block, near Añelo, Neuquén province, Argentina

— Casualties Two workers dead after a severe decompression at a gas separation plant

— Operator YPF, in a 50/50 joint venture with Pampa Energía dating to 2013

— Probable cause Failure in a high-pressure gas line, according to preliminary reports

— Context Second Vaca Muerta incident in August, after a Chevron explosion injured three on 10 August

A failure in a high-pressure gas line triggered a severe decompression at a separation plant near Añelo, killing two workers in Argentina’s flagship shale play.

Two workers died on Tuesday, 25 August 2026, after a severe decompression at a gas separation plant in the Rincón del Mangrullo block, operated by state-controlled energy company YPF in the Vaca Muerta shale formation of Neuquén province, the company and Argentine media confirmed. The YPF Vaca Muerta accident prompted a large-scale emergency response and put contractor safety in the fast-growing basin under renewed scrutiny.

A drilling rig at a shale operation in Vaca Muerta, Neuquén province. Photo: Continental Resources

What happened at Rincón del Mangrullo

The incident occurred on Tuesday afternoon at the Rincón del Mangrullo block, a gas-producing area near the town of Añelo in Neuquén province, at the heart of the Vaca Muerta shale formation. Initial reports from the scene suggested an explosion, but the cause was later clarified as a strong decompression inside a gas separation plant, apparently triggered by a failure in a high-pressure gas line, according to Neuquén-based outlet LM Neuquén. The outlet later reported that a 12-inch pipe had burst at the USP 2 primary separation unit in the block’s northern sector, hurling a metal fragment that struck one of the workers.

Emergency crews, medical personnel and police were dispatched to the site in a large-scale operation that included an airlift of the injured man, local media reported. One worker died at the scene and the second, gravely injured, was flown for urgent medical treatment; hours later, outlets including Noticias Argentinas and TN confirmed the second victim had also died. Both men were working as supervisors at the facility, according to LM Neuquén, which later identified them as Jonathan Meliqueo and Cristian Latorre. It was not immediately confirmed whether the blast wave had injured other workers at the site.

YPF Vaca Muerta accident: company activates emergency protocols

YPF confirmed the fatalities in statements carried by Argentine media. The company said it immediately deployed its emergency teams and activated the corresponding protocols, adding that, regrettably, one employee of the company died and another was transferred by air to receive urgent medical attention. Hours later, the company confirmed the second death: YPF regrets to report the death of the second employee, in circumstances that are being investigated, a spokesperson said, adding that the company had made itself available to the families of both workers.

YPF said the incident was already under control and that the company would update the situation as additional information became available. It did not immediately name the victims or detail the condition of the high-pressure gas line involved, and no official investigation had been formally announced at the time of publication.

Provincial authorities in Neuquén, which oversee oil and gas operations in the province, had not issued a detailed statement on the causes by Wednesday afternoon. Under Argentine practice, workplace fatalities typically trigger parallel reviews by labor inspectors and, where hydrocarbon facilities are involved, by provincial energy regulators, in addition to the company’s own internal inquiry.

It is involved in the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbon fields and production of…

Union response and the victims

The Sindicato de Petroleros Privados de Río Negro, Neuquén y La Pampa, the main private oil workers’ union in the region, clarified that the victims were not workers covered by its collective bargaining agreement. Even so, the union said it deployed its team and health network to respond to the emergency. According to LM Neuquén, union representatives also said the two men had tried to operate something that did not correspond to them, without elaborating.

The union said it regretted the accident and was accompanying the families of the victims, according to statements carried by Noticias Argentinas and LM Neuquén. Labor and energy authorities in Neuquén are expected to review the circumstances of the YPF Vaca Muerta accident, which comes amid a rapid expansion of activity in the basin and growing scrutiny of contractor safety practices.

What is a decompression event?

Gas separation plants receive raw production from wells under high pressure and split it into gas, liquids and water for processing and transport. The pipes, valves and vessels involved operate at pressures far above atmospheric levels, and the gas inside them stores large amounts of energy.

A decompression event is the rapid, uncontrolled release of that pressure. When a high-pressure line or vessel fails, the stored energy is discharged almost instantly, generating a blast wave and hurling fragments that can be lethal to anyone nearby, even when no fire or explosion follows. That distinguishes it from a slower leak: it is the speed of the pressure release at Rincón del Mangrullo that made Tuesday’s incident so destructive.

Safety questions shadow Argentina’s shale boom

The deaths at Rincón del Mangrullo came barely two weeks after another scare in the basin. On 10 August, an explosion caused by a chemical reaction at Chevron’s battery 1 in the El Trapial area injured three workers, with fragments reportedly flying more than 1,000 meters, according to LM Neuquén. One worker was rushed to a clinic in Rincón de los Sauces and two others were treated for light injuries; Chevron said the three, employed by contractor QSB, had been cleaning a pipeline and were later discharged from hospital.

Rincón del Mangrullo is operated by YPF in a 50/50 joint venture with Pampa Energía in place since 2013, covering 183 square kilometers in central-eastern Neuquén, according to Pampa Energía’s investor relations materials. Vaca Muerta as a whole holds the world’s second-largest shale gas reserves and fourth-largest shale oil reserves, and the formation is central to Argentina’s ambitions to become a significant energy exporter.

YPF, which is majority state-owned, is the largest producer in Vaca Muerta and has staked its corporate strategy on the formation, shifting investment away from mature conventional fields toward shale oil and gas under chief executive Horacio Marín. The company has highlighted cost reductions and record drilling productivity in recent quarters, but Tuesday’s deaths put a spotlight on the human risks behind the basin’s rapid build-out, where activity has surged as Argentina seeks to supply its domestic market and ramp up exports to Chile and Brazil.

The accident struck on the same day President Javier Milei was set to meet ruling-party legislators in Buenos Aires to organize the government’s economic agenda in Congress, a day after defending his economic course before his cabinet, local media reported. Both chambers of Congress had sessions scheduled this week as the government negotiated with allied blocs to advance its legislative priorities.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the YPF Vaca Muerta accident at Rincón del Mangrullo? Preliminary reports point to a failure in a high-pressure gas line inside a gas separation plant, which produced a severe decompression. Early accounts described an explosion, but the cause was later clarified as a decompression event. An official determination is still pending. Who operates the Rincón del Mangrullo block? State-controlled YPF operates the block near Añelo in Neuquén province in a 50/50 joint venture with Pampa Energía, a partnership dating to 2013. The block is a key gas producer within the Vaca Muerta shale formation. What has the union said about the two dead workers? The Sindicato de Petroleros Privados de Río Negro, Neuquén y La Pampa said the victims were not covered by its collective agreement, but it deployed its health network to assist, regretted the accident and said it was accompanying the families.

Four Colombian chefs have secured places in the Latin America and Caribbean regional final of the S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy Competition 2026/2027. It is the first time Colombia has placed this many finalists in the contest.

A Record Showing for Colombian Chefs

The selected chefs are Daniela Díaz Fuertes, Diana Pérez, Heisy Córdoba and Diego Ramírez. Their selection marks an unprecedented moment for Colombian gastronomy on this stage.

The competition is open to chefs aged 18 to 30. It aims to identify and promote the best young culinary talent in the world.

For Colombia, the result signals growing international recognition of its food scene. The country has steadily built a reputation for creative, ingredient-driven cooking.

How the Finalists Were Chosen

Specialists from ALMA, the international school of Italian cuisine, made the selection. They evaluated candidates on technical skill, creativity and personal conviction.

The judges also looked for a belief in the transformative power of gastronomy. That criterion goes beyond plating and technique.

It rewards chefs who see food as a force for social and cultural change. The approach fits the competition’s broader mission of nurturing future culinary leaders.

What Happens Next in Panama City

The regional final will take place in Panama City between 27 and 30 September 2026. The four Colombian chefs will compete against other top young talents from Latin America and the Caribbean.

The winner of the regional final advances to the Grand Finale in Milan in 2027. That global stage brings together the best young chefs from every region.

For the Colombian finalists, Panama City is a chance to showcase their skills before an international panel. It is also a platform for building careers beyond national borders.

The Business Read-Through for Hospitality

Gastronomy competitions carry real commercial weight in Latin America. They help young chefs attract investors, media attention and international job offers.

For Colombia, a strong showing can boost culinary tourism. Travellers increasingly plan trips around food experiences and chef reputations.

Restaurants led by recognised chefs often find it easier to secure funding. Recognition from a global brand like S.Pellegrino adds credibility with partners and lenders.

Why Colombia’s Food Scene Is Rising

Colombia’s culinary identity has deepened over the past decade. Chefs have drawn on the country’s biodiversity, from Pacific seafood to Andean tubers.

Cities like Bogotá, Medellín and Cartagena now host ambitious dining rooms. Young chefs are pushing beyond traditional recipes with modern technique.

The S.Pellegrino result reflects that momentum. It also gives the next generation a visible benchmark for what is possible.

What to Watch After the Regional Final

The Panama City event will reveal which chef represents the region in Milan. Investors and food media will watch the outcome closely.

A Colombian winner would further raise the country’s culinary profile. Even without a win, four finalists already signal a shift in regional influence.

Expect more attention on Colombian ingredients and restaurant concepts in the months ahead. The competition often accelerates careers and business opportunities.

Brazilian pianist Leonardo Hilsdorf is set to perform in São Paulo and Curitiba in late August 2026. The concerts highlight both his solo work and his collaboration with a leading chamber orchestra.

A Dance-Focused Recital in São Paulo

The São Paulo performance takes place on Tuesday, August 25. It is a solo recital titled “Diálogos em dança”, or “Dialogues in Dance”.

The venue is Estação Motiva Cultural / Sala São Paulo. The programme is built around works connected to dance.

Composers on the bill include Carlos Seixas, Ronaldo Miranda, Chopin, Villa-Lobos, José Siqueira, Tia Amélia, and Astor Piazzolla. The selection spans Brazilian and European repertoire, from Baroque-era Seixas to the tango-inflected Piazzolla.

Orchestral Dates in Curitiba

Hilsdorf then travels south to Curitiba. He appears with the Orquestra de Câmara de Curitiba on August 28 and 29.

The performances are at Capela Santa Maria, a historic chapel known for its intimate acoustics. Hilsdorf is listed as piano solo for these dates.

With the orchestra, Hilsdorf and trumpeter André de Souza Pinto perform Shostakovich’s Concerto for piano, trumpet and strings No. 1, conducted by Roberto Ramos. The 1933 work is known for its humour and its tongue-in-cheek nod to Beethoven in the final piano cadenza.

Why This Matters for Brazil’s Cultural Scene

Classical music remains a steady draw for educated, urban audiences in Brazil. São Paulo and Curitiba both maintain active concert seasons supported by public and private funding.

For expats and international visitors, these events offer a low-barrier entry into Brazilian cultural life. The venues are central, and the programmes mix familiar European works with Brazilian composers.

Hilsdorf’s dual-city schedule also reflects how Brazilian musicians build careers. They often pair a major-market recital in São Paulo with a strong regional orchestra date in the south.

The Rio Times Lens: Culture as a Soft Asset

Cultural programming is part of the quality-of-life calculation for professionals considering Brazil. Cities with reliable classical music scenes tend to attract and retain international talent.

For investors, a vibrant cultural calendar signals urban stability and disposable income. It is a soft indicator that complements harder data on jobs and real estate.

These concerts are not headline economic events. But they are the kind of recurring activity that makes São Paulo and Curitiba liveable, connected cities.

What to Watch Next

Ticket availability and exact start times are typically announced closer to the dates. Interested listeners should check the venues’ official channels.

The Shostakovich concerto pairs two soloists in a compact, high-energy showpiece. It is a rare chance to hear the work live with a chamber orchestra in an intimate venue.

Hilsdorf’s choice of Brazilian composers such as Villa-Lobos and Tia Amélia also matters. It keeps national repertoire in front of audiences who might otherwise hear only European classics.
