World.title: How to leak a travel piece
World.content:
“Up early and reading an online story about British pubs by Herald travel expert Ben Groundwater, I was astounded to see two embedded ads for GROUNDWATER DRILLING SERVICES, illustrated with a gushing pipe,” notes Mark Southcott of Thirroul. “By 7.45, news of this vital service had gone – humans may have intervened to challenge the ad-matching computer – but should we warn Ben?”

“I was excited, as a teenager, to be taken to Parramatta RSL with my parents for a rare celebratory meal,” recalls Maureen Partridge of Baulkham Hills. “Just as our main courses arrived, two men approached and told us to ‘eat up as fast as you can and then leave’. Our sin? My World War II veteran father was wearing a collared shirt and jacket but no tie (C8). Sixty years later I still avoid clubs.”

“Seeing reference to needing to wear a tie to get into the Chatswood Charles in the ’60s brought back memories of a liquor licence law where you could only buy a drink after 8pm if you were having a meal,” says Ian Costley of Belrose. “The Charles provided a tiny paper plate with a fish finger, meat ball and minute vegetable item to satisfy the law, at a bargain price. Luckily, there was no requirement to actually eat it.”

“On a morning walk last week I smiled and said good morning to a young woman walking in the opposite direction,” reports Jim Pollitt of Wahroonga. “She also smiled and nodded, then, as she drew level, she said, ‘Do you need a change of clothing?’ Hurriedly checking myself for a possible wardrobe malfunction, I turned to ask her for clarification, only to notice the little ear buds and realise she was talking hands-free on her phone.”

Joe Moore of Blaxland shares his train of thought: “It was reported yesterday that rail passengers were ‘detrained’ after the failure of the Sydney rail network. I assume they were ‘retrained’ when the problems were resolved. Any late passengers would, of course, ‘mistrain’.”

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 8:55pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old girl on Sydney’s northern beaches after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital two days after emergency services responded to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights on Sunday night. They found the girl unresponsive. Loading She was flown in a critical condition to Royal North Shore Hospital, where she died on Tuesday night. Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex.



Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young people’s understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Consent education advocate Chanel Contos said she was devastated by news of the teen’s death: “This just feels insanely preventable.” “There is no safe way to engage in strangulation during sex, and unfortunately, mainly because of pornography, where young people are learning and mimicking scripts from that, this act that was traditionally on the fringes of kink culture has made its way into the mainstream,” the Teach Us Consent founder said. “We need to seriously investigate the impact that pornography is having on shaping the sexual scripts and behaviours of young people.” Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in 2024 that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely.



“And there’s really no reason to think that the effects of strangulation would be any different if the strangulation was consensual or otherwise,” the study’s lead author, University of Melbourne Professor Heather Douglas, said. “Even lower levels of strangulation, it can result in brain injuries like problem-solving difficulties, memory issues, and so on, and that’s without even being made unconscious, so it’s a really serious thing to do.” “There’s such a range of injuries associated with strangulation. Some are permanent, some are fleeting … it doesn’t take much pressure, and it doesn’t take very long, to have really terrible consequences.” Douglas said there were no safe ways to undertake strangulation, and she questioned aspects of consent surrounding it. Among the almost 5000 people aged between 18 and 35 surveyed in the research were reports of consent having been assumed from previous instances of strangulation, consent without an understanding of the risks, and consent influenced by pressure or power differentials, Douglas said.



“A lot of people just want to be normal … and doing normal things in their sex life. “And I think there is a bit of a normalisation of strangulation in many young people’s sex lives,” Douglas said. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. Renee Nowytarger Collective Shout co-founder Melinda Tankard Reist said she’s spoken to thousands of girls who have reported feeling pressured into engaging in strangulation during sex, which has been normalised by pornography and social media. “It’s put forward as something desirable and it can heighten sexual experience, but they’re not learning that, well, actually you could die.



“Young people have a right to know the injuries and the potential life-threatening risk. “This is again, just another fruit of a pornographic education,” she said. The NSW government’s own submission to a recent parliamentary inquiry said depictions of sexual aggression including strangulation in pornography has been linked to increased intimate partner violence, citing research from 2017 by the federal government’s Australian Institute of Family Studies. Federal independent MP Zali Steggall, from the neighbouring electorate of Warringah, said the teenager’s death underscored the need for a national education campaign to tackle misogyny and teach respectful relationships. “My thoughts are with her family, friends and community at this incredibly difficult time,” she said.



“Police are investigating the circumstances of the girl’s death and no charges have been laid. We must allow the legal process to take place. “Regardless of the circumstances of this particular case, the Albanese government itself has confirmed that rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are rising. “The Albanese government must urgently roll out a national campaign ensuring young people receive ongoing sexual health and relationship education.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). World.title: Thirty-four Australians among hundreds missing in deadly flash floods in Nepal
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaTragedy Thirty-four Australians among hundreds missing in deadly flash floods in Nepal Niranjan Shrestha and Sibi Arasu Updated August 27, 2026 — 2:12am ,first published 8:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content. Thirty-four Australians are among hundreds reported missing after an avalanche of ice and rock triggered massive flash floods that swept through parts of Nepal and China on Wednesday, killing at least 98 people and causing widespread damage to villages and infrastructure. Officials in Nepal said 403 people, including 341 foreign nationals, were reported missing. Sunil Sharma, a tourism board spokesperson, said 133 were from India on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. Also missing were 47 from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 24 from Canada, he said. Loading At least 62 missing Nepali citizens were among hundreds of locals trekking in the Gosaikunda Lake area in Rasuwa, coinciding with the local festival of Janai Purnima on Friday, Sharma added. Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told The Associated Press at least 28 police officials were missing.



The prime minister’s office in Nepal reported at least 95 dead. Neighbouring China has reported at least three people killed and 265 missing in a border community in the country’s Tibet region. The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9am on Wednesday (around 1pm AEST), destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. They issued warnings to residents of several of Nepal’s districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Torrential floods swallowed roads, bridges, houses, and power projects in the border areas of Nepal, and triggered a mudslide that hit Gyirong Port, a major land crossing with neighbouring Tibet, cutting roads, communications, and power links to the area. CCTV footage shows the moment the Chinese and Tibetan side of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing, known as Gyirong Port, is enveloped by the mudslide. Social media



It is suspected that an earthquake struck the region and triggered an ice-rock avalanche on the Lhende Khola river in Nepal, causing the floods. The river runs through both Nepal and Tibet. The US Geological Survey had reported a 4.4-magnitude earthquake early Wednesday, about 100 kilometres north of Kathmandu, near the border with China’s autonomous region of Tibet. Police and military personnel were engaged in rescue efforts, although officials have said rescue helicopters would not be able to land in the affected areas until the waters recede. Damaged houses stand precariously near the swollen, debris-choked banks of the Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha “We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts,” said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government.



China has deployed at least 574 rescuers to the land crossing, and India says it was coordinating closely with Kathmandu on rescue and relief efforts. People living in low-lying regions were being moved to safer places, and those along the river have been advised to remain alert, as authorities warn that a second flood may occur since a blockage is still lodged upstream. View post on X Flood alerts have also been issued in the Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, which border Nepal, since several rivers flow down the Himalayas into their plains. The worst-affected area, Rasuwa district, witnessed similar flash floods to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in neighbouring Tibet overflowed as a result of high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people lost their lives, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting the two countries, was damaged at the time.



Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday’s flash flood. Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a victim of flash flooding to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, witnessed maximum flooding Wednesday, they said. “The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group. “In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation,” he added.



The Himalayan region, which crosses Nepal and several nearby countries including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because the area is warming up faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Research has shown that extreme weather events, including heat waves, heavy rains and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region. Members of the Kathmandu research group found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000 primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change. AP, Reuters with Josefine Ganko Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Winter illnesses putting a 'dent' in blood donations
World.content:
The New Zealand Blood Service is seeing a drop-off in donations, as regular donors are benched by winter illness.

It normally needed 5000 donations each week, but that had been a little higher lately - possibly also because of the surge in winter illness.

NZ Blood Service chief executive Sam Cliffe said it was currently "challenging" to meet demand.

"Demand for plasma goes up by 8 to 10 percent a year, and that's extremely challenging to keep pace with.

"But we are certainly seeing a drop off in donations at this point," she said.

"The winter illnesses are really impacting donors ability.

"We completely understand, we don't want people to donate if they're ill, but it does put a dent in our collections."

Requiring donors to be healthy was more about protecting the donors than the eventual recipients, Cliff explained.

"Respiratory illnesses don't tend to be transmitted through blood… but we don't want people who are poorly to come into our centres."

But she encouraged anyone who was fit and healthy to make a donation appointment.

World.title: Christopher Luxon challenged on localism at Kāpiti public meeting
World.content:
The prime minister was challenged and complimented in equal measure for his government's local government reforms, at a public meeting on the Kāpiti Coast.

While banging the drum on rates caps drew strong support, Christopher Luxon's answers on the government's amalgamation reforms got a more tepid response.

Luxon had made the short trip over Transmission Gully on Wednesday night to talk health, education, tariffs, and the environment, as part of his now-regular 'fixing the basics and building the future' tour around the country.

The standing-room-only meeting at a Paraparaumu church was a considerably quieter affair than some of Luxon's other public meetings of late, with police only roused to deal with a car that had gone into a ditch in the carpark.

A small handful of protestors outside waved Palestinian flags, but none made it inside, a contrast to the scenes at Luxon's public meeting in Christchurch a week prior.

The crashed car. RNZ / Giles Dexter

Instead, Luxon got free rein to deliver an uninterrupted, 30-minute long speech, starting with a tribute to Dolly Parton.

"This morning I played 9 to 5 to my team at 8 o'clock in the morning at our special meeting," he said.

Luxon acknowledged while many people in the room would be National voters, there would also be people who would never vote National, or who were non-political.

"We're all here tonight because we ultimately all care about where the country is going. We may debate the best way to get there, but we do believe in the ends, and that's visible by the number of people that are here in the room tonight," he told attendees.

Those who stepped up to the mic afterwards quizzed Luxon on cancer care, the government's environmental track record, the fuel crisis, and whether he had hope for the next generation.

He was also asked whether an apology from Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) chief executive Nic Blakeley was enough, following the release of the Privileges Committee's report.

Luxon repeated his answer from earlier on Wednesday, that it was "utterly unacceptable", but the matter was best left to the committee.

"The Privileges Committee made that determination, rightly or wrongly, and the individual at least has apologised," he said.

"I appreciate, a brand new CEO in a very big ministry within a six-month period, badly advised by his officials. But irrespective, I expect better from the public service."

MBIE Chief Executive Nic Blakeley faces MPs in a Privileges Committee hearing into whether he misled Parliament. VNP / Phil Smith

But there were also questions on local government reform, coming from opposite ends of the debate.

One person asked why the rates cap could not kick in sooner.

Councils had to start considering the target range from 2027, but the full 4 percent cap would not take effect until 2029.

Luxon did not directly answer the question, instead explaining why the government was pursuing rates caps in the first place, and pulling out his long-repeated criticism of a public toilet block in Wellington as an example of councils focusing on nice-to-haves over the must-dos.

"Some councils are actually doing a very good job across the country and are working really intentionally to make sure that their rate increases are very little, but others have been in the order of eight to 12 percent increases," he said.

"I don't know whether you noticed, but the opposition parties all hate it," Luxon also said - incorrectly, given Labour has offered its support at first reading.

Later, local councillor Bede Laracy asked Luxon to justify his previous commitments to localism, given how much time the government had spent telling councils what to do.

Laracy told Luxon that at a public meeting three years ago he had given an "excellent" answer on localism and devolution on power.

"At this stage, three years later, I'm not convinced that's what's happened. In Kāpiti, we're looking at the prospect of one of your ministers forcing us to join Wellington, which I have to say is not very welcome," Laracy said, to affirmations around the room.

Christopher Luxon takes questions from the crowd. RNZ / Giles Dexter

Kāpiti Coast District Council has rejected amalgamating with other Wellington-area councils, instead looking to form a unitary authority.

Luxon insisted there were "no predetermined outcomes", and the government had only just received fast-tracked 'Head Start' amalgamation proposals from councils.

"You've obviously chosen not to participate in the Head Start programme, or find a partner or collaborator that you want to do that with. We will now dissect all the Head Start stuff that's come out of the proposals where councils are wanting to work together in different ways and with partners, and we will see what we learn from that experience that might inform how we think about the backstop," Luxon replied.

"But there's no predetermined outcomes taken here at all. I appreciate locally, people will be pretty fired up, and there might be a bit of scaremongering going on. But we've got a wee way to get through this process."

He was also asked why the Local Government (System Improvements) Amendment Bill was taking so long to pass.

That bill would remove the wellbeing provisions from councils, explicitly directing councils to focus on "core" functions.

Leader of the House Louise Upston, who was also present, said she was "under increasing pressure" to get bills through the House.

World.title: Our Changing World: Cold water swimming: panacea or peril?
World.content:
.

Follow Our Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts.

On a frosty mid-winter morning in Alexandra in Central Otago, the outdoor pool temperature sits at just 3.8 degrees Celsius. The grass crunches underfoot and patches of ice have been salted for safety because, incredibly, people are getting ready to enter the water.

This is the 2026 New Zealand and Oceania Ice Swimming Championships. To qualify as an ice swim, the water must be below 5 degrees. Forty-three competitors aged between 16-71 have gathered in Alexandra to compete in different swim style and length categories.

And with them is a small team of researchers from the University of Otago.

Cold water swimming seems to be increasingly popular, fuelled in part by social media claims that it yields a huge range of benefits.

But as more people take the plunge, researchers are trying to better understand what is really happening to the body, and whether the benefits outweigh the risks.

Supporters, time-keepers, stroke-counters and 'seconds' gather around the pool to cheer on the swimmers. RNZ / Claire Concannon

'It's a real buzz'

For competitor Susan Sherwen, ice swimming is about much more than the challenge of cold water.

"It's the friendships and the community that evolves around this event and any ice swimming because you've got to look after each other."

An Auckland science teacher, Susan helped establish the championships six years ago and is a key member of the close-knit community of swimmers.

"It's such a brutal environment," she says. "You often need someone to help you get dressed. That's the sort of intimate contact that just builds really strong bonds."

Her science background and her past involvement organising the championships are why she also put her hand up to be one of the research participants for a University of Otago study.

Event director Laetitia Berten's in one of the early morning heats at the ice-swimming championships. Marijn Wouters

Do experienced swimmers feel how cold they are?

Exercise physiologists Professor Jim Cotter and Dr Kate Thomas are interested to see whether peoples' perceptions of how cold they are and their level of comfort line up with their actual core temperature.

Kate says: "That's important because there's a lot of evidence around how cold people get and it's very variable, very dependent on body shape and size and experience. But how their feelings align with that is less well known."

One theory, which Jim and Kate developed from observing a weekly swimming group called the Frozen Seadogs in Dunedin, is that more experienced swimmers are less likely to perceive just how cold they are getting as they build up a tolerance. Thus, increasing the risk of suffering from hypothermia.

To investigate this, Susan and other participants completed questionnaires about their swimming experience, had their body composition measured, and swallowed a core temperature pill several hours before the longest race of the championships - a one kilometre race, which would see competitors in the water for just under 20 minutes.

Masters student Riley Gould is using pill-sized temperature loggers to track the changes in core temperature of the swimmers during and after their swims. RNZ / Claire Concannon

Masters student Riley Gould is poolside during the race, taking measurement of the competitors' stroke rate.

She then follows up with participants in the designated recovery room afterwards, asking about how cold they feel and their comfort level with the cold, as they sit shivering, attempting to warm up.

Due to a phenomenon known as 'afterdrop', this is when the body temperature is at its lowest.

Professor Jim Cotter explains that cold blood in the periphery is sent back to the heart when the person gets out of the pool and starts to walk around, lowering the core temperature further. That's also why these competitors will avoid warm showers and will instead sit rugged up in the recovery room, sipping on warm drinks.

Alongside investigating this risk of a difference between actual to perceived temperatue, the team are also using a blood prick of the ear lobe to see whether heart stress proteins are elevated after the swim.

What about the benefits?

There are so many claims on social media about the positives of cold plunges and cold water swimming but, says Dr Kate Thomas: "When you look closely…There's not strong evidence really for many of those benefits."

Reducing inflammation, boosting metabolism, mental health effects, the list goes on.

There are other groups that are looking into some of these aspects, and it's likely that there are differences between the risks and benefits experienced by people who are doing short-term cold plunges versus longer cold water swims, Kate says.

"And we're definitely not experts on all of that stuff, but we're hoping to get a little bit more information around the benefits and the risks of a sport that's clearly becoming more popular."

In the benefits column, the team is investigating whether cold-water swimming boosts the levels of brain health related proteins. To do this they will compare protein levels from blood samples taken from cold-water swimmers to those of indoor pool swimmers.

Honours student Emma Maultsaid prepares a blood sample for later analysis. RNZ / Claire Concannon

They won't have all the answers, says Jim, but they're hoping to add a little bit more to what we know. "It's an unusual environment for humans to willingly spend that much time in and we're simply not designed for it. So, it is a responsibility to just try and get more evidence around, well, what are the risks versus benefits?"

World.title: Fatal crash shows 'terrible consequences' of speeding while intoxicated - coroner
World.content:
A Christchurch man's death in a high-speed crash illustrates the "terrible consequences" of choosing to drive at excessive speed while intoxicated, a coroner says

Kyle Eru O'Brien, 30, was going twice the speed limit and was more than three-and-a-half times over the legal blood alcohol limit when his ute barrel rolled, hit a power pole and broke through a fence on 16 November 2022.

He was also ignoring a court-imposed ban on driving at the time.

That evening he had spent more than three hours drinking at the Yaldhurst Hotel and taken diazepam, which he had not been prescribed, associate coroner Stephen Burdes said.

O'Brien's partner and friends left the hotel about 9.25pm and began driving towards Christchurch in a Mazda, with O'Brien following in his white Mitsubishi ute.

"The vehicles were overtaking other cars using the painted median strip. The Mazda was in front; Mr O'Brien's ute was behind," Burdes said.

One witness cited in the coroner's report estimated O'Brien's ute was about 20 centimetres away as "zoomed past" their car on State Highway 73, while another said it flashed by at "incredible speed".

"I was travelling at or slightly below the posted speed limit which is 60kph. I would estimate the vehicle was driving at 120kph," the witness said.

"All of a sudden after the white vehicle went past me and past the vehicle in front, it appeared to flip onto its side, possibly the driver's side. I do not know what caused the vehicle to flip on its side but I heard a loud bang and scraping sounds."

The crash happened about two kilometres from the hotel, Burdes said.

Police found O'Brien might have swerved sharply to the left to avoid an oncoming vehicle.

Two off-duty police officers who arrived just after the crash found O'Brien trapped in the vehicle with his head resting on the roof, Burdes said.

Fire and Emergency and Hato Hone St John paramedics arrived shortly afterwards to cut O'Brien free and provide first aid - however, he did not recover and was pronounced dead at the scene.

The cause of death was recorded as multiple blunt force injuries and possible respiratory compromise.

Toxicology reports showed O'Brien had a blood alcohol level of 179 milligrams per 100 millilitres of blood, well over the 50 milligram legal limit for a driver in New Zealand aged 20 years or over, Burdes said.

O'Brien had also taken diazepam which could have exacerbated the depressant - or brain-slowing - effects of the alcohol, he said.

Because of previous drink-driving convictions, O'Brien had been banned from driving a year earlier for at least 28 days or until he applied for an alcohol interlock licence, which he had not done.

"I cannot say why the two vehicles were travelling at excessive speed, why they were overtaking other cars along the median strip, or why Mr O'Brien drove while grossly intoxicated (having also consumed diazepam) and while disqualified. All I can say is that Mr O'Brien's decisions that evening led directly to his death," Burdes said.

Burdes said there was little he could add to existing public messaging about the dangers of speeding and impaired driving.

World.title: Man charged with human trafficking accused of deceiving staff recruited from overseas
World.content:
A man charged with human trafficking and migrant exploitation is accused of deceiving staff recruited from overseas by promising them they would be paid for all hours they worked.

One of the staff - who was recruited from India - is alleged to have been paid 36 hours per week despite working a minimum of 54 hours.

The man, listed as a company director, is also accused of failing to pay staff for working public holidays, inciting staff to breach conditions of work visas and altering employment agreements to reduce the pay rates.

RNZ earlier revealed a Christchurch man, who has interim name suppression, faced 35 charges under the Crimes Act and Immigration Act.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Immigration New Zealand (INZ) earlier confirmed the charges, which relate to 11 complainants, include allegations of "trafficking in persons and migrant exploitation".

Court documents seen by RNZ reveal the man, aged in his 50s, faces three charges of arranging, organising or procuring the recruitment of a person into New Zealand "knowing that recruitment involved one or more acts of deception".

Two of the complainants were from India, and the third from Saudi Arabia.

The court documents say the defendant recruited them knowing that the terms and conditions of their employment would be "materially different" from what was promised verbally and in their individual employment agreement "namely that all hours he worked would be paid by the employer".

The man also faces charges of supplying information to an immigration officer knowing that it was false or misleading, inciting or procuring people to breach the conditions of their work visas, and failing to pay minimum wage.

He also faces two charges of obtaining by deception by altering the original terms of an employment agreement to reduce pay rates.

One court document says that between November 2020 and June 2022 the man is accused of employing at least five people before their visas were approved.

INZ national manager of investigations Jason Perry earlier told RNZ the charges related to the alleged exploitation of 11 people.

"Trafficking in persons and migrant exploitation are serious offences that can have a significant impact on victims. INZ is committed to identifying, investigating and prosecuting this offending where there is sufficient evidence to do so."

Perry said the charges followed a "complex investigation" by INZ's immigration compliance and investigations team.

"As the matter is now before the courts, we are unable to make any further comment on the allegations, evidence, or the defendant at this time.

World.title: Person assaulted, vehicle shot at after car crash between Toyota and Volkswagen
World.content:
A person has been seriously assaulted and a vehicle shot at following a crash in South Auckland, police say.

They said a Toyota and a Volkswagen crashed about 5.10pm on Ronwood Road in Manukau.

Senior Sergeant Aji Basra said an occupant of the Toyota was then reportedly assaulted by occupants of the Volkswagen.

Police believed a firearm was also discharged, damaging the Toyota.

"Two people received minor injuries, one of which required medical attention and has self-transported to hospital.

"The victims are understandably shaken by the incident, and we are providing them with support."

The offenders left the area in the Volkswagen before police arrived, and in tandem with a Nissan, Basra said.

The Volkswagen was found abandoned on Cavendish Drive, and police believe the offenders continued on in the Nissan.

Their enquiries were continuing.

Serious injuries after Far North crash

Meanwhile, Far North police said it appeared there were serious injuries after a two-vehicle crash in the rural locality of Peria.

Emergency services were called to Oruru Road, near Jason Road, about 8pm.

World.title: Landlord not aware of any issues with pool's gate before child's death
World.content:
The landlord of an Auckland property where toddler drowned says he was not aware of any issues with a pool's gate prior to the child's death.

River Albert-Wihone had only recently turned one when he was found in the backyard pool at his family's Lynfield home. He was taken to Starship Children's Hospital where he died in his mother's arms 12 days later.

The property's landlord Vinesh Natali gave evidence to Coroner Alison Mills at Auckland District Court on Wednesday.

The court was told Natali mostly lived overseas while property management company Crockers looked after the home for the majority of the family's tenancy. However, a different agent took over in the months leading up to River's death.

Natali was questioned by a lawyer assisting the coroner, and also by counsel representing River's grandmother Christine Robinson, who was the main tenant of the home used by multiple generations of the family.

Wednesday's hearing focused on the events of January 2022, when Natali - through Crockers - arranged for fences to be built around the pool in order to comply with new regulations.

Natali said that during conversations with Robinson around the time the pool fence was put up in January 2022, he was not made aware of her concerns about the gate.

"She said poor workmanship and so on. I don't think it was specific to the gate opening or closing, or which direction it was opening or closing," Natali said.

He said he told Robinson that Crockers managed the project and any workmanship concerns should be left with the contractors who carried out the work.

The conversation ended there, he said.

Natali said that after construction was completed the fence passed Auckland Council compliance checks in February 2022.

Earlier, the inquest heard that the pool had failed compliance inspections over a period of four years prior to the family moving there in 2020.

A man from a fencing company who examined the pool fence gave evidence that the tragedy could have been avoided if the gate had been installed with better quality hinges and latches.

Natali was questioned by lawyer Danielle Kelly about whether he'd had any input into the products selected for the job.

"Do you have any comment about concern to keep the cost down? Were you concerned to keep the cost as low as possible?" Kelly asked.

"No, I think as long as the costs were reasonable," Natali replied.

"I don't think I set a clear budget for it either, it was what the cost came in, it looked reasonable."

Lawyer Lucy Wright, acting for River's grandmother, asked Natali about a message he had sent to her client about the construction of the pool fence, in which he had said: "Whatever is cheaper."

"Whichever is cheaper doesn't mean it's cheap cheap," Natali said.

"It's a cost benefit as well, it doesn't mean because it's supposed to be cheap, you go and do the cheapest element. We would obviously look at what would be the most cost effective option that was going to be put in," he explained.

Asked about the pool's history of non-compliance, Natali said Crockers started managing his property in 2015, and that they would tell him if any repairs over $200 were required.

River's grandmother Christine Robinson earlier told the inquest she had raised concerns about the pool fence in January 2022, including an intermittent fault with the gate.

Robinson said she had raised this with the builder, with Crockers and with Natali, but she felt that her concerns fell on deaf ears.

Natali was asked if he knew about landlords' obligation to ensure the safety of the swimming pools even if after they've passed compliance checks.

"I would've relied on Crockers to continue to check it in every visit or whatever that they did at the time," he replied.

Natali was asked if, with the benefit of hindsight, he thought he had an obligation to test the pool gate during an inspection he did in October 2023, a month before River's death.

"Possibly," Natali replied.

After Wednesday's hearing, Natali released a statement to RNZ:

World.title: National and Labour spar over how to help struggling NZers get ahead
World.content:
National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds have sparred over their approaches to help struggling New Zealanders get ahead.

The finance spokespeople were speaking at the Politik election summit on Wednesday.

Politik editor Richard Harman had asked Willis and Edmonds to lay out their economic vision, and what they saw as the context for the election campaign.

The pair agreed the economy was not where they wanted it to be, and their challenge was to create the economic conditions to help "mum and dad" get ahead.

Edmonds spoke about her own electorate of Mana, where she said people could no longer afford the "slap up meal" of mince on toast, with prices rising excessively.

Willis said it was irresponsible of Edmonds to say she was focused on the price of mince, "unless you have a policy to address the price of mince, and I haven't heard that from the Labour Party".

National's approach to help people get ahead was to control inflation, she said.

Edmonds said that did not cut it.

"When you know what it's like to only have $8 in your hand and you are sweating when you take your car to get a warrant of fitness ... It is really difficult to speak to people and say, 'well, we're going to work on the economy here, and eventually that'll help trickle down'."

Edmonds said Labour was focused on making other things cheaper for people, pointing to its policies to cap public transport fares and offer three free GP visits.

She also referenced the former Labour government's pay equity scheme, "which was to help our lowest paid women who look after our babies, look after our grandparents in the retirement homes, who are the plunket nurses, who are the midwives."

The National-led government tightened the scheme considerably, making it harder for people in female-dominated workforces to apply to be paid on par with men doing similar jobs.

The debate descended over that, with Willis and Edmonds speaking over each other to get their points across.

"The fact now that they cannot apply for a pay equity claim to help lift their wages, that's terrible," said Edmonds.

Willis said that was not true, and women could still apply.

"Good luck finding the $11 billion (to pay for the scheme)," she said.

"We don't think it's the government's job to fund pay settlement for private sector businesses ... your position is that the taxpayer in Porirua who can't afford mince on toast should be paying more tax so that Ryman Healthcare can get a pay equity subsidy."

Edmonds responded: "Those Ryman Healthcare workers, if the market was working, why are they on the minimum wage?"

They also had a tit-for-tat over Labour's campaign policy to slim down the government's Investment Boost, which allows businesses to deduct 20 percent of the cost of a new asset, over depreciation.

Labour would target it to small businesses only.

Willis said Edmonds had supported Investment Boost, and suggested the Labour finance spokesperson had lost an argument with leader Chris Hipkins over the policy.

Edmonds said there was no debate between her and Hipkins about repurposing Investment Boost.

"Yes, it's a good policy, but my policy is better, so that's where we've left it," she said.

But Willis said it had been a "frustrating debate" and a "phony war" with Labour which she said had continued attacking the government but not offered up its own fixes.

However Willis said that war ended on Sunday when Labour "finally" announced its fiscal strategy to increase spending to 33 percent, which she calculated would see every New Zealander pay $100 more in taxes each week.

World.title: Nikita Tszyu says Ben Mahoney 'edged' thrilling Gold Coast draw
World.content:
Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney have fought themselves to a standstill in thrilling contest that was scored a split decision draw on the Gold Coast on Wednesday night.

Incredibly, Tszyu said after the fight that he felt Mahoney edged it and should have been given the win.

"I gave the fight to Ben, honestly," Tszyu said in the ring.

"Maybe one or two rounds more, but I can't be a judge. It was a close fight, but I thought he edged it."

Moments later, Tszyu walked back those comments, saying he was emotional and over-critical at himself.

"I think it was just the emotions," Tszyu said.

"I saw myself stopping him. Not being able to get it, that was just a bit emotional for me.

"I'm a huge critic inside the ring to myself."

He did note that it was the toughest fight of his career: "What do you think?" he said when asked.

The judges scored the fight wildly differently, with Phillip Holiday awarding the fight to Tszyu, 117-111 Sabrina Kerr going the other way and scoring 113-115 to Mahoney, while Carl Zappia scored it a 114-114 draw.

"I don't want to talk down on Nikita and his team, but I do believe I won that fight," Mahoney said.

Ben Mahoney took the fight to Nikita Tszyu in the contest. (Supplied: Main Event)

Mahoney was lifted into the air by his team at the conclusion of the fight, clearly believing he had done enough, and stood on the corner waving at his home crowd before the decision was read out.

The fight was desperately even, with Mahoney more active, while Tszyu delivered more power punches.

Both men were marked after the fight, with Tszyu particularly bruised at the press conference.

Regardless of the result, the number five and number seven ranked super welterweights in the IBF both delivered a terrific performance in front of a thoroughly engaged crowd.

The prize for the winner was a chance to face British fighter Josh Kelly for the IBF world title.

A draw somewhat ends those plans for the moment and, with neither fighter seemingly keen to meet in a rematch, it appears the world title ambitions of both may have to wait.

On the undercard, Cal Peters delivered another sensational result, beating Blake Wells by eighth round stoppage to move to 9-0 and win the IBF Pan Pacific middleweight title.

Peters, a 2024 Olympian and silver medallist at the 2022 Commonwealth Games,

"Those country boys, they're just built different," Peters said.

"I was hitting him with some good shots to the head and he just wouldn't go down."

Kirra Ruston beat Saundre Simmons by first round TKO to move to 10-0, much to the disgust of the Bermudan fighter and his corner.

Koen Mazoudier also kept his hopes of meeting Jermall Charlo by beating Sam Beck by majority decision in a tense contest, while heavyweights Brandon Grach and Ike Pluto started the main card off in fine fashion, with Grach winning by split decision.

Follow all the action live from the Gold Coast Convention Centre.

World.title: Giants star Toby Greene opens up on his AFL future
World.content:
Expecting to make a call on his future in the next two weeks, Greater Western Sydney captain Toby Greene has detailed his plans to meet Geelong and Essendon.

Greene, the greatest player in the Giants' 15-year history, is closely considering finishing his career in Victoria so he has more support for his young family.

Admitting it will be the toughest decision of his career, the 32-year-old denied he had already made up his mind to leave GWS.

"I felt like a lot of people in Melbourne, or friends, maybe even some people at the club, feel like I'm definitely going, which is not true," Greene told the Ausmerican Aces podcast.

"If I was definitely going, I'd say that now. I'd be up front with the Giants and make it easy for them."

Giants not sweating on Greene's future The Giants are keen to retain Toby Greene, but they are happy to wait until the 32-year-old is ready to make a call on his future.

Greene's good friend and former GWS teammate, Jeremy Cameron, looms as a natural attraction at Geelong.

Wooden spooners Essendon are desperate for senior stars to help their young talent develop.

Former Giants assistant Mark McVeigh has just been appointed Bombers coach and wants to talk with Greene.

"I'll meet with Geelong probably this weekend, I'd say," he said.

"I couldn't give a f*** about the tour, to be honest. I couldn't care about what their footy club looks like. They're a bloody good club.

"I'd do weights at Anytime Fitness, if I have to.

"'Spike' (McVeigh) has reached out as well since he got the job and asked to catch up.

"I said I'd catch up with him, but it wasn't exactly what I was thinking all year at all."

GWS missed finals for the first time since 2022, with several experienced players already making an exit.

Coleman medallist in 2024 Jesse Hogan, enigmatic forward Jake Stringer and ruckman Kieren Briggs are confirmed departures.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"If I didn't think the Giants would finish top-four next year, I wouldn't stay," Greene said.

"One thing I want to do with them is win a flag and that's the best thing I could do ever in footy.

"I could win two or three (premierships) somewhere else [but] it wouldn't be as good as one at the Giants."

Greene has played 282 games for GWS, including the club's first AFL game in 2012.

AAP

World.title: Time to 'recalibrate': Olympic figure skating champion Liu to miss season
World.content:
Olympic gold medallist figure skater Alysa Liu has said she will sit ​out the upcoming season to fine-tune her technique but reassured fans she would return to the sport.

Liu became ​the first ‌American woman since 2002 to capture Olympic gold in women's singles at this year's Milano ‌Cortina Games, where she also helped ⁠the United States to gold in ‌the team event.

"I ​always want to ‌challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve," Liu wrote in a social media post, ​adding ‌that she would take time to "recalibrate".

Loading Instagram content

"It's important to me that my sport ⁠reflects my personal ‌growth.

"So fear not, I'll ‌be back, and in the meantime I'll be ‌rooting for my teammates near and far."

In an interview with ‌NBC ​Sports on Tuesday, ⁠Liu said she was planning to work on her "overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything" during her break from competition and ⁠intended to return in the 2027-28 season.

Winter Olympics live blog Alysa Liu becomes the first American woman to win singles figure skating gold in 24 years, completing her comeback after retiring in 2022 when she was only 16 years old.

"I just felt this ‌was ‌right. So I'm trusting my ​instincts," she said.

The announcement marks the latest change in a roller-coaster career for Liu, who arrived at the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics and finished sixth.

She won bronze at the world titles a few months later before "retiring" from the sport at the age of 16, saying that skating "takes up your whole life, almost".

When she returned to skating she had a new look, with bleached stripes in her hair and a frenulum piercing — and a new approach and confidence that saw her win the world title in 2025 before gold at Milano Cortina.

Liu said her new approach to her sport and to life was more important than results.

Now she leaves to dream it all up again.

Reuters / ABC

World.title: Hird has chance to finally deliver true unity Essendon seeks
World.content:
When new Essendon coach Mark McVeigh was flanked by president Andrew Welsh and CEO Tim Roberts at his introductory press conference on Wednesday, there was a clear theme emanating from the day: unity.

Unity is the thing Essendon has strived for, and failed to find, for the last two decades as it has cycled through players, coaches and administrators in a bid to end an infamous finals drought.

Welsh hopes that by hiring McVeigh he is able to kill two birds with one stone.

McVeigh to canvass Hird return as icon urges Bombers fans to unite Mark McVeigh and Andrew Welsh are set to approach James Hird about a role at the club after he was overlooked to return as the senior coach for a second time.

The process to find its next coach acted as a litmus test for Essendon to actually show it had changed as a club after years of saying it with no actions to follow.

When Brad Scott was ousted midway through the season and James Hird launched his candidacy on national TV in the same week, the consensus was that Hird's return to the Bombers coaches box was a fait accompli.

The lack of belief or trust in Essendon as a sporting organisation left candidates pulling out, believing the club's trumpeted 'process' was actually a sham designed to deliver Hird the role.

It proved to be anything but, as Hird himself revealed after being beaten by McVeigh, leaving both he and Essendon at a potentially pivotal crossroads.

This rejected bid to be Essendon's coach is completely different to Hird's last rejection, when he finished second behind Brad Scott.

James Hird (centre) was left on the outside looking in when Brad Scott (left) won Essendon's coaching race in 2022. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire)

There was something symbolic in Hird, one of Essendon's favourite sons, being beaten out by Scott, a nemesis of his from the Brisbane Lions heyday.

Scott winning the coaching race was reminiscent another occasion where he'd famously got one over Hird, overpowering the under-cooked then-Essendon skipper on the wing during a key period in the 2001 grand final.

Scott, having arrived from the AFL and being selected by an independent panel, appeared a choice that was an aggressive attempt to get away from the fabric of Essendon.

Scott's regime brought a lot of change, and while his decisions may eventually age well, they left Essendon's diehards feeling more disillusioned with every loss that followed.

Andrew Welsh (left) and Mark McVeigh (right) are keen for Hird to return to the club in an official capacity. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Hird wasn't exactly forbidden from returning to Essendon while Scott was in charge, but he also wasn't welcomed with open arms.

This time around is different as both McVeigh and Welsh prepare to launch full-court presses to get Hird back through the doors, just not as the coach.

While the knock on Hird's coaching bid was his lack of experience in a recent AFL coaches box, what cannot be disputed is his knowledge of the game.

If Hird is able to get past the itch of being the coach, he could prove to be an incredible asset as either a football boss, or as a developmental coach. The opportunities are endless, given Essendon has basically wiped out its entire football department.

James Hird (left), Dean Solomon (centre) and Mark McVeigh (right) have the opportunity to link up under one roof again. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Having held the belief that McVeigh would have come with him had he been successful, as he also pledged to do in 2022, Hird now has the chance to repay the favour.

Welsh has hinted at Essendon bolstering its football department with key appointments in the coming months as it looks to surround McVeigh with a strong staff. It could do worse than bringing Hird back into the fold.

It is notable that Hird, while not receiving the job he wanted, mentioned he has experienced healing during the process in the form of mending fences with individuals he had fallen out with over the club's supplements scandal.

Hird is smart enough to know what his decision from this point on has the potential to do to his beloved club.

As Essendon desperately seeks unity, Hird's return would guarantee it, and he knows that. It is hard to see him turning his back on Essendon to try and coach elsewhere, even if that means he never gets to coach again.

At the front of Hird's mind will be two scenarios: winning Essendon's next premiership, but not as the coach, or winning a premiership elsewhere as the coach. He must figure out which of those will make him happiest.

The benefits of the McVeigh hire are two-fold for Essendon.

He has spent significant time in the coaches' boxes of two teams that have enjoyed deep September runs, albeit without winning the whole lot.

Loading Instagram content

McVeigh's history of working with both the Allies and the Swans Academy was a major selling point given Essendon's list demographic.

Critics suggesting McVeigh's hire was simply a case of jobs for mates were disrespectful to both his decade of coaching reps as well as Welsh's ability to be a professional.

Contrary to all the hysteria about Essendon only hiring "Essendon people", McVeigh is the first Essendon person to be hired as the club's senior coach since Hird's departure in 2015.

The coaches that have followed Hird — John Worsfold, Ben Rutten and Scott — have all enjoyed success at other clubs like McVeigh has, but lacked an ability to truly connect with the club and its fans.

That is McVeigh's superpower. He connects, and he connects with all generations.

It was not by accident that the club filmed McVeigh being greeted at The Hangar by Ken Fraser, the captain of Essendon's 1965 premiership side.

It was also not by accident that both McVeigh and Welsh continually referenced the goal for Essendon to be "one club", making a pointed note to invest in the club's AFLW program.

McVeigh even appeared on a podcast with some of Essendon's biggest content creators from outside the club, a stark difference from Scott, who gave off the vibe of an untouchable CEO fans could never really connect with, rather than your friendly local head coach.

Matthew Lloyd (centre) has indicated he would potentially join McVeigh (left) and Welsh (right) back at Essendon. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

It is no surprise that McVeigh's arrival has already seemingly caused a change in tune from both Hird and fellow Essendon icon, Matthew Lloyd.

Since his retirement at the end of 2009, Lloyd has mostly stayed away from the club while becoming one of the AFL's most prominent media figures.

Lloyd is uncompromising when it comes to his views on Essendon, annoying segments of the club's fanbase who wonder why he has not stepped in to help fix the problems he keeps highlighting.

As McVeigh's appointment grew closer, Lloyd curiously changed his tune and said he would like to go back to club land.

It would be no surprise to see him in an official role at Essendon in the coming years as McVeigh builds out his staff.

All of this brings us back to Hird and Essendon's seemingly never-ending quest to find unity.

The basic pitch from Hird's supporters is that he is the only one who can truly bring unity back to what has been a broken club.

The pitch just missed one thing.

Who says Hird can only bring unity as Essendon's coach?

World.title: Pogačar's sensational solo attack squeezes Vuelta rivals dry
World.content:
Four days is all it took for Tadej Pogačar to end the Vuelta a España as a meaningful contest, the Slovenian great once again riding away from the peloton to win solo and establish a massive lead over the rest of the field.

It has been 32 years since Tony Rominger led a grand tour from start to finish when he won the 1994 Vuelta.

But with yet another thrilling display of daring, Pogačar put himself in pole position to emulate the Swiss rider and become just the ninth man to lead a three-week race from start to finish.

Superlatives have long been superfluous when writing about this Slovenian superstar.

Things that should not be possible are made to look routine.

When he hits the front of a race as the road goes into the mountains, the rest of the pack knows that their only chance is to ride at their own tempo.

Any attempt to fly too close to this generation's greatest star will surely send their hopes of finishing the race crashing to the ground, like Icarus.

As soon as Tadej Pogačar is in this position, that's likely to be the last the peloton sees of him. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Pogačar took off with just over 50 kilometres remaining of the 104.8km circuit around Andorra la Vella to claim yet another dominant victory.

Decathlon CMA CGM put the power down at the bottom of the Collada de Beixalis climb, the second mountain of the day, and ripped the peloton to shreds.

Australian Jay Vine led the charge in support for the Slovenian's UAE Emirates XRG team, but with the pace already high, Pogačar upped his rate to burst clear.

Decathlon's Austrian leader Felix Gall tried to match Pogačar's pace in the initial throes of his attack.

However, the Austrian, as so many riders have discovered before him, could barely hold the double-world champion's wheel and quickly dropped off before being joined by the rest of the favourites.

"The pace was already super fast on the throttle right from the base [of the climb]," Pogačar told media after the race.

"When Jay let me pass him on Decathlon's wheel, I knew: 'OK, I don't want to get isolated from all those general classification contenders, because otherwise they'll all gang up on me.'

"I tried to attack on the climb. When I saw that I could open up a gap, I just hoped I could hold on until the finish. It worked out.

"It was really tough, but it's a wonderful feeling."

Tadej Pogačar is irresistable. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

Pogačar's lead extended to over 3 minutes at one stage before he rolled home to win by 2 minutes and 39 seconds from Jarno Widar, with Gall third.

The 50km attack was his longest in a grand tour, bettering the 43km solo victory he launched in the Pyrenees last month at the Tour de France.

It is another remarkable performance from the Slovenian to add to the extraordinary wins that have become so normal it is expected of him.

Why these people believe in 'freak' Tadej Pogačar's victories As Tadej Pogačar continues to mop up cycling's biggest accolades and most controversial record, one former doper believes he's found the answer to his success: he is just a "freak".

With two key objectives to come this season, the World Championships road race in Canada falls just two weeks after the Vuelta's conclusion, with the Giro di Lombardia a further two weeks after that, Pogačar may now be able to take things easier through the next two-and-a-half weeks of racing in Spain.

The 27-year-old's lead in the general classification now stands at 3 minutes and 21 seconds, with four-time Vuelta winner Primož Roglič sitting second.

"To be honest, any lead is a bonus," Pogačar said.

"This is fantastic, because now I can head into the coming days with peace of mind and a lot of confidence.

"We're taking it day by day and staying focused. Hopefully, after this stage, the pressure will ease up a bit."

Pogačar is also a comprehensive leader in the points and king of the mountains classifications.

Wednesday's fifth stage is a hilly 173.3km ride from Falset Costa Daurada to Terres de l'Ebre in Spain's north east.

World.title: Ex-NBA player who claims to be a woman banned by WNBA team after joust
World.content:
The Chicago Sky has banned Enes Kanter Freedom from its home games after the former NBA centre was ejected from Sunday's (Monday AEST) loss to the Indiana Fever.

Owner Michael Alter made the announcement at a rare news conference on Tuesday, local time. Alter told reporters Kanter Freedom is not allowed inside Wintrust Arena for Sky games "unless sometime in the future, he's able to prove to us that he's able to abide by our rules without being a potential threat".

Kanter Freedom was removed from Sunday's game after a confrontation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.

Cunningham's trans stance opens WNBA up to its latest hijacking atempt Sophie Cunningham insists she wants to protect the sanctity of women's sport, but her comments have opened her league up to an unprecedented attack.

Kanter Freedom was sitting along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female".

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then chest-bumped teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning and walking in Kanter Freedom's direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter Freedom, 34, as she approached him. Kanter Freedom, who was standing, held his arms out and stepped onto the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved between the two.

"It was pretty clear to us that his purpose of coming here was trying to be provocative and see how much attention he could get," Alter told reporters from the Chicago Sun-Times and other media outlets.

Kanter Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing the arena.

"I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN!" Kanter Freedom wrote on social media. "Let that sink in, AMERICA!"

Kanter Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women. But a person familiar with the decision told the AP on Monday, local time, that they are not eligible. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the situation.

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.

Although the league's collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

AP

World.title: CTE study finds 70pc of head impacts happening in sports practice
World.content:
At least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), according to a new study.

Out of the 878 former players who died during that timeframe 235 donated their brains, researchers said, with 215 of those donated brains found to have CTE.

The study's lead author Daniel Daneshvar, the chair of physical medicine and rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said it was difficult to determine how common CTE was as it could only be diagnosed after death.

"People who donate their brains are more likely to donate if they have some concern, some reason for donating, if they think that either they or a loved one is having problems with their memory or thinking or concentration or behaviour changes," he told ABC News Breakfast.

Former NFL players donated their brains to the study and 215 out of 235 were found to have CTE. (Getty Images: Nic Antaya)

"And so you can't just look at the rate of CTE amongst people who donate to get a sense of how common this disease is."

Dr Daneshvar said the "possible prevalence of CTE" among NFL players was "very concerning".

"In the general population, less than 1 per cent of people get this disease pathology in their brain," he said.

" What we found is, at a minimum, 25 per cent of these NFL players died with this disease process. "

The study from Mass General Brigham, Boston University, and the Concussion & CTE Foundation also found dementia was common among brain donors, with researchers urging prevention measures that focus on cutting down on repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport.

"Similarly, we and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population," Dr Daneshvar said.

"The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn't occur at the NFL level.

Here's what we know about CTE The brain disease is caused by repeated head injuries. It's most commonly associated with athletes in contact sports, but there's a lot researchers are still trying to learn about it.

"They occurred at the collegiate level ... and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level.

" And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk. "

The NFL's 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement limited the number of contact practices during the season. The Ivy League banned full-contact tackling during practices five years later.

The Supreme Court cleared the way for the NFL's settlement of concussion-related lawsuits with thousands of retired players in 2016.

An NFL spokesperson said the league continuously strives to make the game of football safer, "including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts".

"The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust — and expanding — set of resources to enhance their physical and mental wellbeing," they said.

"We encourage former players to utilise these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health."

Dr Daneshvar urged current and former athletes experiencing cognitive symptoms to seek a neurodegenerative disease expert evaluation.

"If the changes that have been implemented at the NFL level, including reducing the amount of contact in sports practices to less than one per week, were propagated at the collegiate, high school, and youth levels, athletes would be better off," he said.

"We know that nearly 70 per cent of head impacts are occurring in practice.

"So without changing a single minute of game time at any of those levels, we can be substantially reducing the cumulative head impact burden that these individuals are experiencing throughout their lives."

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Tomic's main draw drought continues as Australians struggle at US Open
World.content:
Bernard Tomic's seemingly unending quest to fight his way back into another grand slam main draw has fallen short once again at Flushing Meadows despite one more worthy scrap from the veteran Australian.

The last time the 33-year-old managed to battle into a main draw of a major was at his home Australian Open in 2021.

In the five years since, he has entered 10 more qualifying events in the slams and failed to negotiate his way through any.

Alas for the former teenage wonder boy who got to number 17 in the world a decade ago, that drought continued on Tuesday afternoon, local time, in New York as he fought back in his first-round match against South African Lloyd Harris only to be outplayed in the final stanza.

No-one can possibly fault the effort of world number 179 Tomic, who was once perceived as being a talented but undisciplined figure who did not really care enough about the sport, as he has since battled on in the lower reaches of the game around the world, tirelessly seeking another day in the sun.

Emerson Jones also failed in her bid to advance to the women's main draw despite a valiant fight. (AAP: Darren England)

But Harris, a former world number 31 himself who is still dangerous even if his ranking has fallen to 139, just had a little too much for the Gold Coast veteran, who staged a second-set fightback before going down 6-2, 5-7, 6-2.

It was the same story for a couple of other Australians in first-round action, as teenager Emerson Jones fought valiantly to peg back Dutch world number 164 Suzan Lamens in a tight second-set tiebreak, only to succumb in the decider 7-5, 6-7 (7-9), 6-2 after two hours and 25 minutes.

With another veteran, Alex Bolt, losing 7-6 (7-3), 7-5 to Spain's Pablo Llamas Ruiz, it meant that Australia were still looking for their first winner of the week in qualifying after James McCabe's loss on the opening Monday.

At least one Aussie was guaranteed a place in the second round of qualifying as Storm Hunter took on her friend Maddison Inglis later in the day.

AAP

Tech.title: Apple announces September iPhone launch event
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple’s next launch event will take place on September 9th at 1PM ET. Invites to the event, which has a “Surprise and shine” tagline, were sent out on Wednesday. The event will take place at the Steve Jobs Theater in Apple Park, but there will also be a livestream.

September’s show could be a big one, as Apple may finally announce the long-rumored foldable iPhone. A photo of a dummy unit indicates the foldable may have a wide form factor that’s similar to what Samsung used with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, a phone that our reviewer Dominic Preston said “feels like the future.”

Apple is also expected to refresh its Pro and Pro Max phones, but those are rumored to be iterative upgrades and not a big redesign like Apple announced last year. Should past trends continue, they’ll likely be called the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

However Apple reportedly won’t announce the base model iPhone 18 at the event and instead introduce it next year. In 2027, Apple is also rumored to be launching an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air.

This event will also be the first with John Ternus as Apple’s CEO. Formerly the company’s hardware chief, Ternus is set to take over from Tim Cook on September 1st.

Tech.title: Volvo’s cars will warn one another about hazards in the road
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Volvo is updating three of its electric vehicles with new hazard alerts to warn drivers when there are animals or vulnerable road users ahead. The new connected safety features are based on Volvo’s cars talking to one another, as opposed to crowdsourced alert systems used by popular navigation tools like Google Maps and Waze.

The alerts work by using connected vehicle data from Volvo’s fleet of passenger vehicles in Europe, the US, and Canada. The car’s sensors and cameras are tuned to identify certain risks on the road. When one Volvo spots a hazard, it automatically logs the location and sends it to Volvo’s servers. Alerts are then sent to all other Volvo vehicles traveling along that same road. The alerts still depend on the car being connected to the cloud and the road existing in the map database, but Volvo’s newer EVs have plenty of computing power to handle the real-time processing requests.

Previous Next









1 / 6

Volvo said it’s updating its EVs with alerts for four types of hazards: large animals; vulnerable road users, like pedestrians or cyclists; roadwork; and accidents. The new alerts are coming to the Volvo EX90, ES90, and EX60. Volvo says it has 1 million vehicles on the road today with connected safety alert capabilities. And it shares its alert data with traffic management centers, as well as other vehicle brands, so its not just Volvo branded vehicles that are benefiting.

Volvo has used connected vehicle technology to power some of its hazard warnings since 2016. The Swedish company’s cloud-based system, developed in partnership with Ericsson, warns drivers of slippery roads ahead based on feedback from steering, braking, and acceleration sensors. It also notifies nearby vehicles when another car has activated its hazard lights indicating that another driver may be in a dangerous or unexpected position on the road.

In addition, Volvo said that the EX90 would be getting Spatial Audio support for Apple CarPlay users. This will allow drivers to “enjoy a multi-dimensional and immersive sound experience that places music and vocals around the cabin,” the company says.

Tech.title: Xbox announces disc-to-digital feature that digitizes your physical games
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is officially announcing a new Xbox feature that will allow Xbox owners to digitize their existing physical game collections. The disc-to-digital feature, which The Verge exclusively revealed last month, is part of work that Microsoft is doing for game preservation and in preparation for the next generation of Xbox consoles.

“Most Xbox One and Xbox Series X disc-based games support this new feature,” explains Jason Ronald, VP of next generation at Xbox. “Players can claim a digital entitlement by inserting a supported disc into an Xbox One or Xbox Series X console and launching the game.” This digital entitlement is tied to the specific disc, and it will move from account to account if you swap the physical game with a friend or log in to a different Xbox profile and try to play a disc-based game.

Microsoft will start testing this new Xbox disc-to-digital feature with Xbox Insider testers on August 31st, followed by a broader rollout to Xbox One and Xbox Series X consoles in the coming months. Once you have a digital version of an Xbox disc game, if supported you’ll also be able to access the game on PC through Xbox Play Anywhere, or stream it to multiple devices with Xbox Cloud Gaming.

A leaked memo from earlier this month revealed that publishers would have control over the Xbox disc-to-digital, so not every game will be supported initially. “We’re starting with thousands of titles, and we’ll continue to add more over time,” says Ronald. “While not every title will be available at launch, this is an important step toward a future where players can have greater confidence that the games they buy remain with them for years to come.”

The Xbox disc-to-digital feature arrives just weeks after Sony announced it’s killing all physical PlayStation game discs. New PlayStation games released after January 2028 will be digital-only, but it’s not yet clear if Microsoft will announce a similar end of production for Xbox discs. Either way, Sony hasn’t announced a similar feature for converting an existing physical library into a digital one.

Microsoft is also bringing Xbox and Xbox 360 games to PC, in a move that could allow the next Xbox console to play every Xbox game ever made.

Under the special-edition shell, it’s an Xbox Series X with 1TB of storage.
